Most visitors to Hawaii stick to one island because interisland flights add $100-$400+ per person to the trip cost. By using points for these short hops, you unlock a fundamentally different Hawaii experience — island-hopping from Oahu to Maui to the Big Island to Kauai without the airfare costs stacking up. This is a multiplier strategy: you are not just saving on one flight, you are enabling an entirely different type of trip. Combining a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight with points-funded interisland hops creates a nearly free (in cash) multi-island Hawaiian vacation.

Decide which islands you want to visit and in what order. The most common combinations are Oahu + Maui, Oahu + Big Island, or a three-island itinerary. Map out how many interisland hops you need so you know the total points required.

Check Hawaiian Airlines (7,500 miles each way), Southwest (variable, typically 4,000-8,000 points), and United (5,000-7,500 miles) for each interisland segment. Southwest often offers the best flexibility with no change fees and no blackout dates.

For Hawaiian Airlines, transfer Amex Membership Rewards. For Southwest, earn Rapid Rewards directly or transfer from Chase (transfer to Southwest is currently limited). For United segments, transfer from Chase or use Turkish Miles&Smiles for even lower pricing.

Book each interisland hop as a separate one-way award. This gives you maximum flexibility to mix airlines and optimize pricing per segment. One-way awards have no penalty compared to round trips on these short routes.

Align your interisland hops with your arrival and departure flights. Arrive on one island and depart from a different one (open-jaw booking) to avoid backtracking. For example, arrive Honolulu, hop to Maui, depart Maui to the mainland.

Hawaiian Airlines has the most extensive interisland network and offers the most daily frequencies. Southwest Airlines also operates key interisland routes (Honolulu-Maui, Honolulu-Kona, Honolulu-Lihue). United flies select interisland segments as well. Each airline has different award pricing and transfer partner access.

Hawaiian Airlines interisland awards typically price at 7,500 HawaiianMiles each way. Southwest varies by cash fare but generally costs 4,000-8,000 Rapid Rewards points each way for interisland hops. United interisland segments can be booked for 5,000-7,500 miles using various Star Alliance partner programs.

Yes, especially when booking multiple hops. A family of four making two interisland hops at $150 each way would spend $1,200 in cash. Converting that to points frees up significant cash for accommodations, activities, and dining. The per-point value (1.5-2.5 cents) is reasonable, and the trip flexibility gained is substantial.

A popular strategy is to fly into Honolulu (Oahu), hop to Maui for beaches and Haleakala, then continue to the Big Island (Kona) for volcanoes and snorkeling, and optionally finish on Kauai for dramatic scenery. Each hop is 30-60 minutes. Allow 2-3 days minimum per island.

This redemption was built for families and couples planning a multi-island Hawaii vacation — full stop. If you're visiting multiple islands (which most Hawaii first-timers and repeat visitors do), you're already mentally budgeting for interisland flights. This sweet spot simply redirects that cash budget back into your pocket and replaces it with points.

Families get a 5/5 Family Friendly score here for good reason: availability is wide open, booking is simple, and the economics scale beautifully. Four people, two hops = 60,000 miles to cover potentially $1,200+ in interisland airfare. That's an extraordinary displacement of vacation cash.

Beginners are explicitly welcomed by this redemption's design. There's no partner airline complexity, no fuel surcharge math to calculate, no routing rules to decode. You search on Hawaiian's website, you transfer points, you book. The 5/5 Beginner Friendly and Easy to Book scores reflect that this is genuinely one of the simplest award redemptions you can execute.

Minimum points needed: 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person per segment. For a solo traveler doing two hops, that's 15,000 miles. For a family of four doing two hops, that's 60,000 miles.

This is NOT for: Travelers who don't have an Amex MR or Bilt account and no path to earning HawaiianMiles quickly. It's also not ideal for travelers who only need a single interisland flight — the opportunity cost of setting up the transfer relationship for 7,500 miles may not be worth it unless you're already accumulating MR points for other redemptions.

This redemption earns a **Beginner** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. In a world of waitlists, fuel surcharges, routing rules, and phone-only bookings, Hawaiian interisland awards are refreshingly clean. **What makes it easy:** Award availability is consistently excellent (5/5). The booking portal is functional and user-friendly. There are no fuel surcharges to calculate. Miles never expire, so there's no pressure. You can complete the entire redemption — from transfer initiation to confirmed booking — in about 48 hours. **The one genuine friction point:** Earning HawaiianMiles isn't as straightforward as earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex MR. Hawaiian doesn't have a widely-used co-branded credit card for most people's everyday spend. This means you're dependent on transfer partners, and the Amex MR and Bilt paths are your primary options. If you don't have either, this redemption becomes harder to access. **Tip 1:** Start with an Amex card that earns Membership Rewards — the Amex Gold is the ChooseFI community favorite for everyday earning. Once you're accumulating MR points, you have a direct path to Hawaiian via a 1:1 transfer. **Tip 2:** Always search award availability before transferring. It takes 30 seconds and protects you from the one mistake that could derail an otherwise smooth booking. **Tip 3:** Don't overthink the merger situation. Hawaiian and Alaska remain separate programs today. Book what's in front of you. If you can earn Amex MR points, you can execute this redemption. It's the perfect first award booking for a ChooseFI member who wants to see how the system works without risking complexity.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Interisland awards are the key that unlocks multi-island Hawaii vacations without the stacking airfare costs that keep most travelers on a single island. At 7,500-10,000 miles per hop, the points cost is modest, and the trip transformation is significant. Whether you use Hawaiian Airlines miles, Southwest Rapid Rewards, or United partner programs, the strategy is the same: let points handle the short hops so your cash stays in your pocket for experiences. Combined with a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight, interisland awards make a multi-island Hawaiian vacation one of the most achievable aspirational trips in travel rewards.

#8825. Herniated Discs Are a Common Cycling Injury—Here’s Everything You Need to Know

Keep your back health on track with these tips from top docs and bike-fit experts.

Sometimes it happens with a bang, like when former Tour de France pro Marty Jemison was racing Tour of Flanders in the late 1990s. His saddle slipped to be nose up. He thought “no big deal” until one of the steep cobbled climbs, where he was in the saddle cranking out maximum wattage.“And my back just popped,” he says.

Jemison finished the race and the others that followed until he retired about 18 months later, though he had pain off the bike and for the first 30 or 60 minutes of riding, and knew something was wrong. That something was a herniated disc that became nearly debilitating after retirement, eventually required two procedures, and still flares up to this day if he’s not meticulous about his bike position and on top of his core work.

Other times, it’s the proverbial straw that breaks the camel’s (or the cyclist’s) back, as was the case with avid long-distance cyclist Mark Elsasser of Philadelphia who developed some sciatica in 2018. He was able to ride through it just fine, but couldn’t sit for any length of time before the pain was unbearable. The diagnosis: a herniated disc in his low back, which he resolved with physical therapy and has kept at bay by changing his position on the bike, going from a 0-rise to 5-degree stem. “My spine is less compromised being a bit more upright rather than nose down on top of the stem,” he says.

Herniated discs are fairly common in the general population, occurring most frequently among 30- to 50-year-old adults, and men more often than women. Interestingly, you may have one right now and not even know it. “We know from radiographical studies that 50 percent of those aged 40 may have some form of disc herniation. We might consider it normal, age-related changes, and many of those won’t be symptomatic,” says bike fitter and sports physiotherapist Bianca Broadbent, co-owner of The Cycling Physios based in the United Kingdom.

In fact, one research review published in the American Journal of Neuroradiology found that degenerative changes in the discs, which include herniated discs, are present in nearly 90 percent of adults 60 and older and often require no intervention. A herniated disc only causes pain if it’s pressing or otherwise irritating a nerve root in the spine

Join Bicycling All Access for more injury-prevention tips and training advice!

Your spine is comprised of 24 vertebrae. Between those vertebrae are fluid-filled cushions known as discs, which act as shock absorbers for your spinal bones.

“Imagine your spinal discs as jelly-filled doughnuts,” says Andrew Pruitt, Ed.D., the founder of the Boulder Center for Sports Medicine and CU Sports Medicine and Performance Center. “A herniation happens when the jelly inside pops out.”

You may hear people using other terms like “bulging disc,” “ruptured disc,” or “slipped disc.” Technically, a bulging disc is just that: It’s when the jelly inside the donut is pushing against the side enough to bulge out from the vertebrae but isn’t leaking out. A ruptured or slipped disc refers to an actual herniation, where the doughnut cracks, allowing the gel-filled center to squeeze out.

A bulging and/or herniated disc can cause pain by creating pressure on the nearby nerves. There’s some evidence that the leaked fluid from herniated discs also can cause chemical irritation and inflammation of the spinal nerve roots.

Again, it’s possible to have an asymptomatic herniated disc where you feel no pain. When you do have pain from a herniated disc, however, you’ll know it.

Pain from the herniated discs is sharp and radiating. Most cyclists experience herniated discs in the lower, lumbar back (we’ll get to why in a bit). So you may feel burning pain often known as sciatica that radiates from your lower back into your glutes and down one or both legs, sometimes even into your feet. You may feel pain similar to an electric shock when you stand or sit or walk. You may also feel radiating numbness, tingling, and/or weakness in your lower extremities.

So how does the jelly get out of the doughnut and start wreaking havoc on your spinal nerves? In a word: pressure. It can be extreme and sudden, like Jemison cranking on the cobbles. Or, in many instances, it can happen gradually over time, as was the case with Elsasser.

When your spine is in its generally straight, neutral position, the pressure from the top down is uniform on your discs, so the jelly inside those cushions is evenly distributed, Pruitt explains.

“When you bend forward, the jelly is pushed back, stressing the skin of that doughnut,” he says. “If you’re sitting all day, that jelly is pressing back there for eight hours. Now jump on a bike, and you add another two hours in an even more extreme position, pressing that jelly further and further, until—pop—it comes out.”

Though herniation can happen anywhere in the spine, in cyclists it happens most frequently in the lumbar (low back) region close to the base of the spine, or the L5-S1, the bottom-most disc that sits right on top of your tailbone, because that’s where we bend the most, says Menachem Brodie, C.S.C.S., head coach at Human Vortex Training and USA Cycling expert coach.

“For many cyclists, the L5-S1 is where they’re getting their flexion, and the lumbar spine has about six degrees of movement,” Brodie says. So if you’re not hinging from the hips and keeping your spine within its safe, natural range, you’re pushing those limits. Keeping your spine under that kind of stress for prolonged periods of time pushes you closer to the failure point.

Along those lines, research shows that riders with a lower handlebar position and greater flexion in that key lower back region were more likely to have low back pain. Though, importantly, the research also suggests that poor core strength and endurance could contribute to the spinal stress and low back pain in cyclists.

Of course, the bike isn’t the only place you can stress your spine. The gym can be another place riders put their spine under unhealthy stress, says Dane DeLozier, D.P.T., the biomechanics lab director at and co-founder of Revo Physiotherapy and Sports Performance. Maintaining a stable, neutral spine is very important when resistance training, especially when doing big lifts like deadlifts and squats as well as under velocity like with kettlebell swings, DeLozier says.

“When you have your spine under load, you want it to be neutral and very stabilized. You want to be hinging through your hips, not bending and extending your spine under load,” he says.

If you’re unsure of if you’re maintaining a neutral spine, DeLozier recommends setting up your phone and recording yourself (or having a friend video record you) so you can see if you are breaking or flexing under load.

The good news is a 2020 scientific paper, “Slipped disc: Overview,” reports that about 90 percent of people will get relief from their pain and restricted movement within six weeks even if they receive no medical treatment. That’s because the body gets rid of part of the prolapsed tissue or it shifts position so that the nerves aren’t irritated anymore, according to the overview.

You can help that process along with physical therapy, DeLozier says. “The vast majority of folks feel better and have a great outcome by doing mobility exercises for the hip and low back and decompression exercises for the spine.”

The exercises you do depends on your individual situation, but your physical therapist may recommend mobility, stability, and core strengthening exercises such as:

Press Up: Lie facedown with your feet together, toes pointed, and your forearms on the floor palms. Pull your shoulder blades down and in towards your spine and press into forearms to lift your chest off of the floor, keeping your neck long and hips on the floor. If mobility allows, you can press up further by placing hands below your shoulders to come into an up-dog position. Hold for 3 to 5 seconds. Repeat about 15 times.

Hip Flexor Stretch: Kneel with the affected knee on the floor, tighten your glutes, and brace your abdominal muscles while keeping your back straight. Pressing hips forward. Hold this stretch for 30 seconds. Do 3 times.

Bird Dog: Get on your hands and knees with your palms flat on the floor, shoulder-width apart. Slowly raise and straighten your right leg and left arm at the same time. Keep your hips aligned with the torso and not tilted to one side. Hold for 10 seconds. Return to start. Repeat on the other side.

Cycling itself, when done with a healthy riding posture, can also be a great rehab tool to strengthen the discs and surrounding structures, Broadbent says. In fact, a study done on high-volume road cyclists who rode nearly 100 miles a week for five or more years had beneficial adaptations to their discs and psoas (the biggest hip flexor muscle), which were beneficial for spinal health.

If you’re riding through your rehab, Brodie recommends “crocodile breathing” when you get off the bike. To do it, lie facedown with your forehead resting on the back of your hands and let your chest and hips sink into the floor. Inhale deeply into your belly, expanding your diaphragm for four slow counts. Pause for two seconds, then exhale for six slow counts.

Finally, while many herniated discs can be treated conservatively with physical therapy, some require injection therapy like nerve blocks, if the symptoms are severe, Broadbent says. In rare cases, spinal disc herniation can cause extreme pressure and swelling of the nerves at the end of the spinal cord causing a medical emergency known as cauda equina syndrome.

“If your bladder and bowels aren’t working properly, you have saddle numbness (off the bike as well), or you have sexual dysfunction such as unable to get an erection then you should seek urgent medical investigation,” Broadbent says.

Again, cycling can actually improve spinal strength and the health and hydration of your discs, says Broadbent.

Having a good bike position and the right saddle is key. “You want your spine in a healthy position that doesn’t strain those discs in your lower back,” Pruitt says. If you ride a gravel or a mountain bike, you’re likely already in a slightly more upright, more neutral spine position, he says.

An anatomical saddle will also allow you to put your weight on your perineum without putting harmful pressure on those sensitive tissues, so you’re able to reach the bars without bending too far and putting your spine in an unhealthy position. “Saddle technology improvements have really helped reduce degenerative disc disease,” he says.

You also can protect your spine by doing core-strengthening exercises several times a week. Brodie recommends what are known as the “big three” exercises for spinal stability, developed by renowned back pain expert, Stuart McGill, Ph.D., Professor Emeritus of Spine Biomechanics at the University of Waterloo. These exercises stiffen the musculature throughout the core in a way that enhances stability in the spine.

How to do these exercises: The American Council of Exercise recommends performing three sets for each using a reverse pyramid rep/set scheme. Start with a higher number of repetitions for the first set, then decrease by 2 to 6 reps, then decrease by another 2 to 4 reps on the last set. So you might start with 8-6-4 reps and work your way up to 12-10-8 reps as you get stronger and build endurance. Hold each exercise for no more than 8 to 10 seconds.

McGill Curl-up: Lie on your back with one leg extended and the other leg bent, foot flat on the floor. Put your hands under your low back to maintain your natural arch. In one move, lift your head, shoulders, and chest off the floor, keeping your neck and back in the neutral position. Hold. Then slowly return to start. Do half a set. Then switch legs and complete the set.

Side Bridge: Lie on your right side, with your forearm on the floor and elbow underneath your shoulder. Bend your knees at a 90-degree angle. Place your left hand on the opposite shoulder for stability. Lift your hips off the floor so your body forms a straight line from your head to your knees. Hold. Then lower to the starting position and repeat to the other side. Work up to doing the move with your legs straight.

The Bird Dog: (As explained in the previous section)

You can make these exercises part of your warm-up, along with dynamic mobility moves before you get into your bigger lifts.

Off the bike, Brodie recommends practicing good spine hygiene by avoiding hunching forward when you sit and not sitting in a static position for prolonged periods of time, but rather shifting positions in your chair every 15 minutes and getting up, moving around, and doing a little standing stretch, extending your arms, reaching overhead and taking a deep breath every 60 to 90 minutes.

Finally, don’t overlook your mattress. A firm mattress with a pillow top will help support your spine while you sleep, Brodie says. “A lot of people overlook this and it can make a big difference in your back health.”

#8824. Can the Tour Be Pogačar-Proofed? The 2027 Tour de France Route Is Designed to Keep the Racing Close.

More time trialing and fewer summit finishes could give Remco Evenepoel, Jonas Vingegaard, and the rest of the peloton a chance to take the fight to the five-time champion.

It’s early November, which means the Halloween candy is on sale, the piles of leaves in my yard are getting harder to ignore, and the routes for the 2027 men’s and women’s Tour de France have finally been unveiled. After weeks of refreshing Tour rumor sites, here’s what stood out to me about the men’s route.

First, let’s address the Slovenian elephant in the room: There’s little anyone can do to defeat a healthy, in-form Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG), who will head into the 2027 Tour as the overwhelming favorite to take a record-breaking sixth overall victory. Certainly, the organizers seem to feel the same way.

Rather than create a race designed to defeat him, which currently doesn’t seem possible, they’ve laid out a course that could at least prevent the five-time champion from running away with it in the first week. The 2027 Tour packs more than 53,000 meters of elevation gain and 28 second-, first-, or hors catégorie climbs into its 21 stages. But there are only three summit finishes, and the first doesn’t arrive until the end of Stage 9, atop the Grand Colombier.

That means fewer chances for Pogačar and his team to jump out to a huge early lead on the Tour’s general classification and then ride defensively, slowly wearing down the opposition until the final week. That’s when the Slovenian usually delivers the coup de grâce, adding a few more stage wins to his ever-growing tally.

Yes, there are a couple of punchy uphill finishes in the opening week, at the end of Stages 4 and 5, and Pogačar will do well on them. But the time gaps shouldn’t be huge, so I expect a tighter bunch of riders at the top of the GC heading into the first individual time trial on Stage 7.

Speaking of time trials, the 2027 Tour features 71 kilometers of them across Stages 7 and 16, the most we’ve seen since 2012. It’s hard not to see that as a nod to Belgium’s Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull–Bora–Hansgrohe), the four-time world time trial champion who finished second in the Tour this past July.

If he can improve his preparation for this year’s Tour, and he’s only 26, Evenepoel could use those time trials to his advantage. The first might even give him a chance to give Pogačar a scare before the mountains arrive at the end of the opening week.

But waiting until Stage 9 for the first mountain stage doesn’t mean the opening week will be easy. A slew of long, tricky stages will be tough for one or two teams to control. And at least until the Stage 7 time trial, plenty of riders should be in contention to spend a day or two in yellow and willing to take a few risks and big swings to make it happen. That’s the downside of designing a route that attempts to delay the GC fireworks until the second week. More riders feel they have a chance to wear yellow, which can lead to more risk-taking and, unfortunately, the possibility of more crashes.

Throw in tight roads, punchy climbs and descents, some rain during the three opening stages in the United Kingdom, and perhaps a few days of crosswinds, and you’ve got the exact right mix to create unpredictable and downright chaotic racing.

If Pogačar is going to run away with another Tour, I expect we’ll know by the end of Stage 11, the final day in the Alps and the second of the race’s three summit finishes. If his rivals, including Evenepoel, Denmark’s Jonas Vingegaard (Visma–Lease a Bike), and France’s Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM Team), can somehow limit the damage on Stages 9, 10, and 11, we could have a much more compelling Tour than what we’re used to.

A run of sprint and transitional stages follows before the final week, when the second time trial and two days in the Pyrenees await. With any luck, we’ll still have a GC battle worth watching by then.

That’s what the organizers appear to be hoping for with this route. But given what we’ve seen from Pogačar and his UAE squad in recent Tours, I’m not sure it will happen. While the time trial kilometers seem to acknowledge Evenepoel as one of Pogačar’s greatest threats, I also see the route as a not-so-subtle gesture to Seixas, the young Frenchman many consider the rider most likely to be Pogačar's successor.

Seixas, now 20, raced his first Tour this past summer and finished fourth overall. The 2027 course should give him a chance to continue growing as a Tour contender without throwing him in at the deep end the way this year’s route did. The French would be thrilled to see him finish on the final podium, and with the Tour’s most intense stages broken into two- or three-day chunks, with time to recover and regroup in between, that kind of result looks well within his reach.

I’m also eager to see how two-time Tour champion Vingegaard tackles the race. Recent routes have forced Vingegaard and his Visma–Lease a Bike team to burn a lot of matches early, leaving them powerless when Pogačar and his UAE teammates throw down in the second and third weeks. The 2027 course should allow Vingegaard to ride a bit more under the radar, hopefully keeping him fresh for the Stage 7 time trial and the first summit finish on Stage 9. If all goes to plan, the Dane could enter the third week ready to challenge Pogačar in a way we haven’t seen since Vingegaard won his second Tour in 2023.

As for specific stages, I’ve already marked a few as days I won’t want to miss.

The Tour begins in the United Kingdom with three stages that should generate some intense battles among sprinters and Classics riders. Of the three, Stage 3 looks like the hardest. Its 223 km route includes a slew of punchy climbs, making it a perfect day for riders like Mathieu van der Poel (Alpecin–Premier Tech), Wout van Aert (Visma–Lease a Bike), and Tom Pidcock (Pinarello–Q36.5 Pro Cycling Team).

Then there’s Stage 10, a 171 km ride from Annecy to Sallanches that features six categorized climbs and previews the course used in August’s world championship road race. Coming right after the Tour’s second rest day and sandwiched between summit finishes on Stages 9 and 11, this should be an exciting and hard-to-predict day for the GC contenders.

Stage 14 takes the riders 199 km from Montpellier into the Cévennes, covering many of the roads immortalized in Tim Krabbé’s The Rider, one of the best cycling novels ever written. Seriously, if you’ve never read it, find a copy and enjoy! The stage ends on an airstrip just past the summit of the Côte de la Croix Neuve, a famous climb that always generates an exciting finish.

After taking a back seat in recent Tours, the Pyrenees close out the mountain racing in 2027, highlighted by Stage 18. The Tour’s “queen stage” runs 174 km from Pau to Saint-Lary-Soulan, with 5,400 meters of elevation gain and perhaps the two toughest climbs in the entire race: the Col du Tourmalet and a summit finish on the Col du Portet. If the race hasn’t been decided heading into Stage 18, it should be by the end, even with one relatively milder day in the Pyrenees still to come.

And what about Stage 21? Maybe you heard the pre-announcement rumors that the organizers would skip the cobbled Côte de la Butte Montmartre. Thank goodness they proved false. Adding a few trips over the climb to the final stage in 2025 has proven to be one of the greatest innovations in Tour history, and I’m thrilled they kept it in for another year.

Overall, the 2027 men’s Tour stacks up like this: 3,479 kilometers (2,162 miles) spread over 21 stages, with seven flat stages, six hilly stages, six mountain stages, two individual time trials, and three rest days.

With about eight months to go before the riders hit the road in Edinburgh, a lot can still happen. Most of the top contenders haven’t even confirmed their 2027 programs, which means there’s a chance, however unlikely, that at least one of them might not participate.

But as long as Pogačar is racing, the result, for better or worse, might be a foregone conclusion. And that’s not necessarily a bad thing. He is a once-in-a-lifetime talent, resetting the record books of the sport the way Eddy Merckx once did.

But as the saying goes: it’s the journey—not the destination—that matters here. Yes, we should enjoy speculating about who will and who won’t win the Tour de France—and how and when they manage to do it. But we can’t forget that the Tour de France offers at least 21 chances for something exciting and unexpected to unfold. Next year’s route might not prevent the inevitable, but it will certainly produce lots of great racing along the way. And I can’t wait.

#8823. What is the Ironman World Record? It’s Complicated

Who holds the Ironman world record? Depending on who you ask, it's Magnus Ditlev and Anne Haug, who own the fastest iron-distance time. (Photo: Ironman (Donald Miralle), Challenge Family, FinisherPix)

After a dramatic DNF in the final miles of the run at the 2026 Ironman World Championship, Magnus Ditlev (DNK) raced at Ironman Florida just four weeks later to post the fastest Ironman finish time ever with a 7:19:17.

That time upended the previous best iron-distance set by Sam Laidlow just a few months prior at Challenge Roth, where the Frenchman finished in 7:21:04 on the course where the fastest women’s race ever is still held by Germany’s Anne Haug from 2024

And yet, despite all these amazing feats, there are no world records in full-distance racing.

Confused? It’s understandable. Pour yourself a cup of coffee and get ready to learn why Ironman (and iron-distance) world records technically don’t exist.

In the world of running, 26.2-mile marathons must adhere to rigorous certification standards set by World Athletics that include restrictions on things like point-to-point courses, elevation drop, and (recent) International measurement, but triathlon operates without such official oversight. Course configurations are notoriously inconsistent, often shifting from one season to the next, and triathletes don’t even think twice about point-to-point courses or elevation drops between start and finish.

Certainly course distances are confirmed in high-level World Triathlon races like the Olympics, but there is no course certification for long-course or for regular age-group races. Often, you’ll hear athletes remark that their GPS watch clocked an Ironman course as short or long – rarely does a race hit exactly 2.4 miles of swimming, 112 miles of cycling, and 26.2 miles of running. Those are ballpark figures that races would love to hit if they can, but permitting issues might mean the host city can only close 110 miles of roads for the bike course – this occurred at Ironman Texas in 2018, when “Ironman record times” were clocked by Melissa Hauschildt and Matt Hanson.

Beyond the logistics, an athlete’s clock is at the mercy of Mother Nature; factors like local climate, hilly terrain, or even a current-assisted swim can skew the data (as was the case in 2021, when Blummenfelt floated downcurrent to a 39:41 swim en route to a then “Ironman record” of 7:21:12 in Cozumel).

Because of that, Ironman confirmed in 2026 that they do not keep track of “official” world records for that reason, with a spokesperson telling Triathlete, “Due to variance of courses (even from year-to-year the same race could have course alterations), combined with the fact that unlike marathons, triathlon does not have official course certification for records, we use world best, course best, race best, swim/bike/run course best, etc.”

The same holds true for Ironman 70.3 races and non-branded half-iron triathlons; no course certification, no “official” record.

For what it’s worth, the Guinness World Records recognizes the “fastest time to complete an Ironman triathlon,” but not fastest iron-distance time (which we’ll explain in the next section). This may be more a function of marketing, as Ironman has established its own “partner” page on the Guinness Book of World Records website. Guinness does recognize some other triathlon records, including “fastest lumberjack triathlon,” which raises many other questions we’ll save for a different article.

Then there’s the branding gymnastics of Ironman™ versus an iron-distance race like Challenge Roth.

You see, even though Challenge Roth is a 140.6-mile triathlon, it’s not an Ironman. Ironman is a distinct brand of 140.6-mile races, though many use the name to designate the distance (similar to how most Americans say “pass me a Kleenex” for tissue, or “I need a Band-Aid,” instead of requesting an adhesive bandage).

And though Challenge Roth has been around for decades, the course and race have evolved. In 2010, the Challenge Roth run course was adjusted to be more spectator-friendly, and the bike course has been altered several times for safety, most recently in 2024. In 2026, Roth expanded the pro bike drafting zone from 12 to 20 meters, creating entirely different race dynamics altogether.

Ultimately, establishing a definitive “record” is difficult even for a single event, given how much can change from one year to the next. And though iron-distance “records” are often broken at Challenge Roth, they’re technically not the site of “the fastest iron-distance times in history.”

In 2022, Kristian Blummenfelt and Kat Matthews covered the 140.6-mile distance in what would have been record-setting times of 6:44:25 and 7:31:54 – except that they did it in a unique setup involving pacers, drafting, and extra equipment as part of the Sub7/Sub8 Project. The event allowed for advanced technological and athletic optimizations, featuring specialized gear like prototype bikes and pace teams on the swim and bike to provide slipstreams for Blummenfelt and Matthews to draft off of — all things you’d never be allowed to do in a legitimate race

This format drew considerable criticism and debate on social media, with the community questioning whether the Sub7/Sub8 times should be viewed as legitimate records. Many referenced Jan Frodeno’s 7:27:53 time for a similar iron-distance experiment known as Tri Battle Royle, which was held on a highly modified course featuring special ramps and a perfectly mapped swim line to remove tricky turns.

Because these events were so heavily optimized, no one regards these times as actual world records — just like the much-hyped 2017 Breaking2 Nike marketing event for the marathon record. Instead, they’re chalked up to fascinating experiments for fans to geek out over. (And for that, we’re thankful.)

So now that we’ve determined there is no official world record for Ironman, iron-distance triathlon, or otherwise, we can establish there are fastest-known times, with all the caveats above.

#8822. Your First Gravel Ride Should Feel Like an Adventure—These 3 Tips Will Help You Enjoy It

Gravel takes different prep than road riding—these basics help you ride off road with confidence.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

The more riders I talk to, the more I see people switching over to gravel bikes. I was leading a group ride for a shop in New Jersey and the group primarily consisted of road cyclists on their first gravel ride. The line of the day was, “this is so fun—it’s like being a kid on a bike.” Gravel is challenging, but it’s also a different type of fun once you get off paved roads.

Over the last few years, I’ve focused more on gravel riding than any other discipline of cycling. My lunch rides typically end up being on the road and my strictly fun rides end up being on the mountain bike. But I’ve been gravitating more and more to the gravel bike because it can do a little bit of everything.

I’ve taken gravel bikes on everything from 100-mile road rides with 10,000 feet of climbing to rides on singletrack trails where we should have been on a hardtail mountain bike at a minimum. On bikepacking routes, gravel day rides, and family rides towing my kids in their bike trailer, the gravel bike has been my go-to rig.

If you’re new to the sport, or even just getting into the category of gravel riding, it's easy to feel like there’s a mountain of knowledge needed as a barrier to entry. Here we’ll break down the top gravel tips you need to know to find success in those first few rides and beyond.

When I ran a shop this was the first place I would start with folks who were gravel curious. The touchpoints on a bike are both where you contact the bike and where the bike touches the ground. The pieces of gear to focus on here are: chamois, gloves, saddle, bar tape, and tires.

The chamois and gloves are the first two because they are the parts on your body that touch the bike. I don’t like to use gloves that are overly padded, but I do like gloves that have a good level of tackiness to help with staying gripped to the handlebars. This year I’ve been using the Most Days Full Finger Gloves from Handup for everything from century gravel group rides to hard gravel rides with plenty of singletrack. The chamois can be a little more subjective, but I almost always suggest going with chamois bibs over chamois shorts.

Bibs stay in place better than shorts and this is especially important from the movement you’re doing on a gravel ride. I’ve had plenty of people ask if they really need padded shorts for riding and the short answer is no. You can go riding with regular basketball shorts, but you’ll have a much better time riding with padded shorts or bibs. I like to compare it to riding a road bike on gravel. You can absolutely do that, and for a long time that’s what people did, but there’s a better way. My favorite pair are the Q36.5 Dottore Pro Bibs because they stay in place incredibly well and are comfortable from the first hour in the saddle to the 11th hour. The price point is a realistic hurdle for these Q36.5 bibs, but our Deputy Test Editor at Bicycling, Tara Seplavy, calls out this pair available on Amazon for just $40 in her roundup of cycling shorts.

I personally like a tape that has some tackiness while also offering a bit of cushion for some dampening after miles of chattering gravel. My favorite tape is the Lizard Skin DSP Ultra Bar Tape. It comes in a range of colors and thicknesses, but I usually go with the 2.7mm or 3.5mm for people riding gravel. If you want a little extra comfort over the miles size up to the 3.5mm.

When it comes to saddles this is much more subjective because everyone’s sit bones are different and your preferred saddle can change depending on your position on the bike. Personally I have different saddles on each of my bikes based on how I use that specific bike. The biggest note on saddles is to avoid going with something super wide and overly padded. This can be a desirable thing to reach for after you’ve developed a bit of soreness from your initial rides, but try to avoid the beach cruiser type of saddles. These can cause extra friction and that’s the last thing you want to add to your gravel ride.

Finally, we get to where the bike touches the ground—the tires. When someone is looking to add comfort and versatility to a gravel bike I usually recommend bumping up the tire size. Most bikes don’t come stock with the widest tire you can fit on the bike, so check the technical specifications for your bike to see how wide you can go. Some of my favorite gravel tires are the Pirelli Cinturato H tires and the Continental Dubnital tires for their versatility on a range of terrains.

This is a broad tip, but it is the most all-encompassing piece of advice I can give for gravel. Gravel riding burns more energy mile for mile and climb for climb compared to a road ride. Keep this in mind when you’re putting together your nutrition and hydration plan as well as when you’re building the route. It’s important to bring more calories than you think you need because you’ll likely be burning more calories compared to a road ride; it will take longer to get to the next refill stop compared to what you would expect, and those refuel spots are fewer and farther between on gravel roads and dirt trails compared to a road ride.

When it comes to setting up my route I always suggest riders have a way to navigate. When I got into gravel riding I used my phone for navigation with a handlebar mount on the bars. This worked initially, but because of the mud on some gravel routes, the possibility of falling, and how fast navigating on my phone killed the battery I quickly switched to a dedicated head unit. Head units that are capable of navigating reasonably well can range from a few hundred dollars to just shy of a thousand. Currently I’m testing the COROS Dura 2 Solar and I love the fact that battery life can last for days of solid run time. A dedicated bike computer head unit is something that’s nice to have as you start to adventure, but if you currently have a smartwatch you can likely use that to navigate for now. It’s more convenient having the head unit in front of you for navigation compared to a smart watch. Lately I’ve been trying a few different watches from Garmin and COROS as a substitute for a bike computer and once I set up turn-by-turn notifications I’ve gotten used to navigating by the watch. Plus I can use the watch for other activities like runs, family hikes, and the occasional paddle.

Flat tires will eventually happen on a gravel ride. Step one is to bring a good flat kit with a reliable set of tire levers, a multitool (with a chain breaker), at least one tube, and a pump for inflation. I also typically bring a dollar bill as a backup for a tire boot in the event that I really blow out my tire. Ever since I had to use fallen leaves as a tire boot I always carry something to cover a large hole in the tire.

Step two is knowing how to use the tools you brought. Bringing a chain breaker tool or tire levers are great, but they won’t be much help if you aren’t able to figure out how to use them. When someone was buying a new bike from me I used to encourage them to practice taking the wheels off the bike, tires off the wheels, tubes out of the tires, then putting it all back together. Getting some laps on this process from the comfort of your home will make the process feel much smoother when you’re trying to finish the flat fix on the side of the trail.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8821. We Tested 15 Electric Mini-Inflators. These Tiny Pumps Are Fast Enough to Replace CO₂ on Many Rides

From 90-gram pocket pumps to premium inflators, these editor-tested picks make flat fixes easier.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Pumping up tires is a constant of cycling. Whether you’re checking pressure before a road ride, fixing a mid-ride flat on your gravel bike, fine-tuning your air pressure at the trailhead, or topping up tires on your kid’s bike in the garage, every cyclist needs to put air in their bike’s tires

Some riders don’t worry about the exact psi in their tires, but others constantly check and analyze their air pressure, and the latter group may be onto something. In his story, “More Speed and Comfort? The Right Tire Pressure Can Give You Both,” Test Editor Dan Chabanov explains that having the correct pressure in your tires provides more confidence and control on rides.

Small, portable electric inflators have recently taken the cycling world by storm and quickly gained popularity with riders. For several decades, traditional pumps (floor, frame, and mini), CO₂ cartridges, and air compressors have been the go-to methods for filling tires. While mini-inflators don’t fully replace these other inflator types, these small electric units are now finding their way into riders’ toolboxes, gear bags, jersey pockets, and seat bags.

Over the last two seasons, we’ve subjected 15 electric mini-inflators to the same tests. We originally tested 11 inflators in 2025. In November 2026, we tested 4 models (from Cyclami, PDW, State, and Lezyne) and updated our Best Mini-Inflators ranking. A handful stand out for specific use cases or rider types. But these are only a few of the great pumps out there; choose the one that best fits your needs and budget.

With svelte dimensions and a 106-gram weight, the Ultra Tiny is small enough to stash in a jersey pocket, flat kit, or bar bag. Plus, it quickly inflates tires of all sizes to pressure. The AS2’s super-accurate gauge also makes it worth considering for your home shop or carrying in a race-day tool kit. However, the pump runs a little hot.

At the media launch for the Colnago G-5X, someone asked the brand representatives if any inflators fit inside the internal frame storage. That led me to search for options that can fit inside frames. The Cyclami A5S came up in some discussions, so I ordered one on AliExpress to test.

Overall, it’s a solid little inflator that performs well—sub-one-minute inflation times and a 122-gram weight. The rounded profile and placement of the air chuck (on top rather than the side) help it squeeze into many frames’ internal storage doors. Of the five road, gravel, and mountain frames in the office I checked, the A5S fit into four (it didn’t fit into the Cervélo Caledonia).

Several Bicycling editors rely on the Air Rush on rides and at home. Overall, it’s a solid and dependable pick. It has a nice display, runs cool, and inflates road and gravel tires in under a minute. It also filled five road tires; that’s better than most units. I only wish it were slightly smaller for carrying in a seat bag or internal frame storage.

Like many RockBros products, this mini-inflator isn’t the best at any single thing, but it does everything pretty well overall. It gets tires up to pressure in under 50 seconds, doesn’t run too hot, isn’t too loud, and isn’t super heavy.

The most expensive model in our test, the Ultimate, lived up to its name, hype, and steep price tag. And matching its durable appearance, this inflator is a beast—it gets tires up to pressure in under 30 seconds and inflates eight tires on a single charge. I tested Silca’s claim that the Ultimate will seat tubeless tires—surprisingly, it succeeded.

The Ultimate was the quietest inflator in our testing and tied for the second-lowest temperature. Other than price, the biggest negatives are the Ultimate’s weight and size. One note: after almost a year of frequent use, an O-ring inside the pump failed. However, Silca offered to replace the unit under warranty.

The Pocket SE doesn’t feature a display or gauge, but at only 90 grams, it weighs less than a single CO₂ cartridge and head. And though it takes roughly a minute to inflate a tire to full pressure, I can fill four tires on one charge. The Pocket SE’s one downside is that without a pressure gauge or a 72 psi cutoff, I’d be cautious using it on hookless tubeless road wheels.

For a year, I’ve carried the Pocket SE in my seat bag for flat fixes, and it has gotten me out of plenty of jams. My only complaint is that the button activates easily; a bump or pothole can trigger the unit if it isn’t carefully positioned in your bag.

Portland Design Works makes well-crafted, usable gear for everyday cyclists. The brand doesn’t take itself too seriously, and its products sometimes have whimsical or quirky elements (like its water bottle cages).

PDW’s Essentials inflator follows this mold—it’s well-designed, looks good, and functions well. The Essentials inflates tires quickly, and the gauge is pretty accurate. Its best feature is presets for different bike types (labeled road, gravel, mountain, and city). You can use these to set your tires for your quiver of bikes, or program them for different rides, wheelsets, or riders in your house.

The screw-on chuck is slightly tricky to use and leaks some air if not fastened correctly. While the unit’s body doesn’t run hot, the hose’s base certainly does: heed that yellow warning tag.

Mini-inflators are pint-sized electric air compressors. Larger electric pumps have been around for many years and are commonly used at home, in the garage, or the workshop. Some people carry electric pumps in their vehicles to air up car or truck tires and fill inflatable rafts or SUPs. Cordless air inflators have been a common sight around World Cup mountain bike team paddocks and cyclocross pit zones for several years.

Yet cyclists only started using these inflators within the last three years, when the prices dropped, the form factor shrank, and battery life increased. Riders soon found electric inflators perfect for the garage or the trailhead. Plus, their smaller size makes them much easier to toss in a bike bag or luggage than a floor pump when flying with a bike.

Several cycling equipment brands have released models tailored to bicycle riders’ tastes and preferences. Some companies have even cut enough weight and reduced the proportions to make electric mini-inflators a viable option for carrying in a jersey pocket or flat kit on rides.

The current crop of bike-specific mini-inflators can be broken down into two groups:

1) Small enough to bring on a ride, and 2) Everything else.

Of course, your definition of “small enough” might vary greatly from another cyclist’s. If you ride with a bar bag or frame pack, an inflator like the Portland Design Works Essentials or Trek Air Rush might be sufficiently tiny. However, if you carry everything in a ride wallet or obsess about weight, even Silca’s 112-gram Elettrico Micro might be too large for you.

For our testing, we focused on mini-inflators sold by cycling-specific brands and ones marketed for bicycle use. This isn’t an exhaustive test of every inflator available; instead, it provides context to help you choose one best for your needs.

In two years of testing, we’ve evaluated fifteen models across a wide price range ($15 to $160). These include mini-inflators from respected cycling brands, options from smaller companies, and those that fly under the radar.

To test if size matters, I picked some based on their tidy proportions and low weight. I also chose a couple of larger, heavier options to see whether they push air significantly faster or fill more tires than other mini-inflators. I also bought the cheapest mini-inflator available on Amazon ($14.90 on the day I was shopping) to test it against the pack and see if spending more on a pump really matters.

As with other Bicycling head-to-head product tests (like insulated water bottles, flared handlebars, and wide road tires), we evaluated electric mini-inflators based on real-world requirements, not intricate lab tests. Riders can replicate at home without much fancy equipment.

We inflated the tires to air pressures for a 180-pound cyclist riding a road, gravel, and mountain bike in average conditions (as recommended by Wolf Tooth’s app). For road riders, we recorded the time to inflate a 28mm-wide tubeless tire to 65 psi. We also measured the time to reach 30 psi on a 45mm gravel tire. For mountain bike riders (or folks riding new-school gravel bikes), we clocked the time to 20 psi on a 29x2.3-inch tire. To evaluate the pumps without built-in gauges, we measured the pressure they reached after 50 seconds.

After timing inflation speeds for each category, I fully recharged all devices. The next morning, I tested how many times each electric mini-inflator could fill a 28mm road tire to 65 psi from fully flat. To prevent overheating, I let each inflator cool down for ten minutes between fills.

In addition to real-world tests, we also measured three common concerns of electric pump buyers: Temperature, noise, and gauge accuracy. For these tests, I borrowed equipment from my colleagues on the Popular Mechanics test team.

This included a specially designed fixture that measures bike pump gauge accuracy. Gauge accuracy is important, especially for riders using hookless tubeless road wheels. Since the maximum allowed pressure for these wheel systems under ETRTO standards is 5 bar (72.5 psi), you don’t want to risk a tire blowing off a rim due to a wildly inaccurate pump reading.

Like other users, I have personally experienced noise and heat build-up issues with electric mini-inflators. Early one morning at Sea Otter Classic, my inflator woke the cyclist in the hotel room next door—my sincere apologies to him! Later, on an All Bodies on Bikes group ride, the inflator I borrowed from another cyclist to change a flat melted the plastic valve of my spare TPU tube.

Lesson Learned: Due to excess heat, always use an extension hose when filling plastic-valved tubes with an electric mini-pump.

“Do I plan to carry this on rides?” you ask when purchasing a mini-inflator. If you answered “yes”, look for lighter-weight and smaller-profile models. If you only plan to use the inflator at home, at the trailhead, or at races, don’t focus on size or weight.

Unless you only need to get out of a jam on the side of a road or trail, look for models that fill more than two tires. This allows you to adjust tire pressure and inflate tires on other bikes or spare wheels (and for friends to borrow before a ride—because you know they will need it).

After evaluating these mini-inflators, my key takeaway is that price doesn’t exactly make it the best for your needs. The most expensive pump in our test has brilliant inflation speed, is the quietest, and doesn’t run hot—plus it fills lots of tires. But it’s too heavy and large for most cyclists to carry on rides. However, spending more doesn’t guarantee better performance either, as some pricier models didn’t outshine the low- or mid-priced models. And, as I found out from testing, you probably don’t want to buy the absolute cheapest possible option either (luckily, this model is no longer available).

Skimming listings for different devices, you’ll notice (from similar design details and parts) that a select few vendors manufacture many electric inflator models for every brand. But even if a mini-inflator shares the same outer silicone protector, case, buttons, or display, it doesn’t mean they’re identical. For example, in our testing, the Rockbros model outperformed the extremely similar-looking Muc-Off Air Mach pump.

Unless you specifically need a lightweight, compact mini-inflator for on-the-bike use, spend a little more for a model with a built-in gauge. A display is super handy, and you can pre-set your desired pressure within 1 psi (some even read to tenths).

Pro Tip: If you buy an inflator without a built-in gauge, time how long it takes to reach your optimal ride pressure from fully flat before bringing it out on the road or trail. Then, when you’re airing up a flat fix, you can count off (or use a timer) to get you relatively close to your riding pressure.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8820. What Yoga Can Teach You About Overcoming Common Obstacles in Life

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about overcoming obstacles in life first appeared in the May-June 2003 issue of Yoga Journal. You can find more of our Archives here.

As we practice asanas (yoga postures) with awareness, we not only feel better, we are also better able to feel. That is, we become more sensitive to everything in our lives. As our sensitivity deepens and widens, we begin to practice asanas in such a way that we are practicing the larger yoga, which is the discovery of our Self and our dharma (our true purpose) and the overcoming of the obstacles that impede this journey.

In the Yoga Sutra, Patanjali explains the five main kleshas (obstacles) on the yogic path. They are avidya (ignorance); asmita, (ego); raga (attachment to pleasure); dvesha (aversion to pain); and abhinivesha (the fear of death). Though there are many yogic methods for dealing with the kleshas, asana practice—both the poses we explore and the manner in which we work in them—can be one of the most powerful of yoga’s tools for helping us overcome these afflictions.

For all these obstacles, hatha yoga has a powerful remedy: backbends. Let us then take a look at the ways in which backbends—and specifically one of the most common backbends, Urdhva Mukha Svanasana (Upward-Facing Dog Pose)—can help us face the kleshas and overcome them.

How can we work on the kleshas while practicing backbends?

In the epic poem Savitri, the Indian sage Sri Aurobindo writes, “Where ignorance is, there suffering too must come.” Patanjali says that avidya, or ignorance, is the father of all the kleshas, so let us begin there.

Because backbends demand such focus, they are extremely powerful tools for overcoming ignorance. In an asana, any part of the body in which awareness is not present when it should be can be called ignorant. And any ignorant part of the body prevents the free flow of energy, causing stagnation. So our work is to bring awareness to the parts that are ignorant, replacing avidya (ignorance) with vidya (knowledge).

Among the asanas, backbends are especially useful in this process, since they require strong concentration and open the chest and heart center.  There are many manifestations of bodily ignorance that show up regularly in prone backbending poses. The most common mistake is to do these poses with the shoulder blades up near the ears. Another common site of ignorance, especially in Urdhva Mukha Svanasana, is the neck. If you are not aware of your neck while doing this pose, you compress your cervical vertebrae and demonstrate once again that “where ignorance is, there suffering too must come.”

Avidya in our physical body also manifests in the mind, which becomes unable to pay attention or retain and recall information. If we are to dispel our ignorance, we must cultivate the ability to focus our attention as well as the ability to calm our minds. Indeed, an unfocused brain cannot be calm. Thus, the ability to focus is a precursor to learning how to make the brain quiet.

As we practice and discover the ignorant parts of our body, our more refined awareness lets us see that these parts are being sacrificed to fulfill the ego. The ego’s desire to gratify itself makes us oblivious to restraint. We plow into poses just so that we can appear to be doing the posture. When we abuse the lumbar spine in Urdhva Mukha Svanasana to get a deeper-looking backbend, rather than slowly strengthening the lift of the pit of the abdomen, that too is ego.

The ego doesn’t care about balance or integrity, because it is more concerned with performance and getting as far as possible as fast as possible. The ego is competitive, yet it feeds itself both on achievement and on self-pity. Whether the ego says, “I am the greatest” or “I am the weakest,” it is all the same: It is all about the “I.”

Backbends also help us overcome the obstacle of asmita, the ego, because they open the heart center, the seat of our connection with our higher Self. Asmita is the mistaken identification of the small, individual self with the universal, supreme Self. The ego believes it knows everything and thinks that the universe revolves around it. As the ego grows, consciousness moves away from the heart and into the brain. Over time, the connection between the mind and the heart—the smaller self and the larger Self—is lost. Backbends help bring us back to this connection.

The ego also blocks our progress in asana, for it assumes we have knowledge where we are ignorant. When we puff out the chest to appear powerful, denying the very weakness in our core, that is ego. The ego makes us believe that we have achieved a certain level of practice when actually we haven’t. It encourages us to practice for self-glory and pride rather than for the discovery of the spirit-self.

To work on the ego is to face the shadow self. The shadow self is that part of us which does not want to go to the light. It is the part we hide so that we can appear to be good. We do not want to face it, because it runs contrary to our self-image and is out-of-sync with our conscience. Yet unless we are willing to uncover and work on our shadow in both our asanas and our lives, unless we are observing our ego’s urge to repress our darker parts, we are not truly progressing on our path.

Backbends not only help us uncover the shadow but also create space for the heart chakra to open. As this happens, we release our egoistic viewpoints and see the basis of others’ thoughts, even when they are opposed to our own. Isn’t this the foundation for creating world peace, one yogi at a time?

In asana practice, as elsewhere in life, we are attached to pleasure (raga) and averse to pain (dvesha). But the true practitioner of yoga understands that temporary discomfort often leads to more stable and permanent pleasure. In fact, our aversion and attachment often stem from confusion. Looking only at the immediate effects of actions, we mistakenly label as pleasurable that which feels good in the moment even if, in truth, its real long-term effect will be painful.

In the practice of Urdhva Mukha Svanasana, for example, relaxing the shoulders and arms may momentarily feel pleasurable, but this attachment to pleasure will, in the long run, cause tension and compression in the neck and collapsing in the chest. On the other hand, pushing down strongly with the arms, contracting the triceps, and using the side chest muscles can initially be painful—it certainly requires strong effort—yet these actions lead to freedom in the neck and expansion in the chest.

Be conscious throughout your practice of Urdhva Mukha Svanasana—indeed, in all backbends—that you do not just fold the spine at a single point or area. Much as folding a paper clip many times at one point eventually breaks the metal, such acute folding of your spine can create compression and damage. The lower back and the neck are especially susceptible to such collapse.

The chest and heart openings provided by backbends also counteract the last three of the five kleshas: raga, dvesha, and abhinivesha. Raga, our attachment to pleasure, is a futile grasping of the ephemeral—we clutch what is only transient. In doing so we close our chest and shut down the heart center. Dvesha, aversion to pain, also closes the door to our hearts. When we cover up pain, we cover up our shadows, the parts of ourselves that we repress because they do not please the ego. As with raga, our aversion is not expressed with open, wide arms but with a clutching, defensive posture.

Abhinivesha, the fear of death, is the father of all fear, the primal cause for all shrinking of the chest, hunching of the spine, and withdrawing back into our small selves.

As we practice Urdhva Mukha Svanasana, how can we work on the final klesha, abhinivesha, the fear of death? By approaching and practicing the pose as though it were new to us every time we come into it. The fear of death is the fear of change; only as we accept change can we turn this fear away and grow. Doing the pose today as we did it yesterday is reenacting a dead pose. Doing the pose according to the inspirations of today gives birth to a pose that is alive.

Yet new life doesn’t exist without the old life dying; we must let go of yesterday’s accomplishments in order to keep growing. Each time we practice asanas in a new way, we work on overcoming our personal fears of death and rebirth, taking another step into a truer and more luminous life.

#8819. Stocking-Ready Tri Gifts $20 and Under

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Summary: The Triathlete editors combed through dozens of websites to find under-$20 giftable triathlon accessories and essentials that will fit in a stocking.

Triathlon has a lot of gear, which usually means high price tags and a whole lot of required storage space. But these compact tri gifts pack a punch in value – they make training and racing safer, more comfortable, or more convenient, and all for $20 or less.

Even better: Some of these products are already on sale for Black Friday and the holidays. So get to shopping — these Santa-approved stocking stuffers will have the triathlete in your life ready to sleigh their next race.

Gift a little swim-spiration with this Rosie the Riveter–inspired message on a latex-free silicone swim cap. You can never have too many swim caps, and this one protects hair from chlorine, keeps goggle straps in place, and makes swimmers visible, especially on open-water swims.

The off-season is the perfect time for a handlebar retape, and triathletes will love this popular tape from one of the oldest brands in cycling. There’s a reason this cork tape has been around since the 1980s – it has the right amount of cushioning, a no-slip grip, and is self-adhesive, making it easy to install. Available in multiple colors, and it comes with black end plugs.

Sure, these belts for holding your racing bibs on the run are not the flashiest, but goodness do they make T2 simpler on race day. They need to be replaced every couple of years as sun and sweat break down the elastic, and this Huub one is great quality. The two toggles for bib attachment are as easy as it gets.

Gu acknowledges that eating energy gels on race day can get a little … sticky. They partnered with Hydrapak to design this 150-milliliter soft flask, which can hold up to five Gu Energy Gels (or three Gu Liquid Energy Gels), can easily slip into a pocket, and offers a high-flow nozzle. This makes a thoughtful upgrade for long-course triathletes who are tired of messy gels!

These nifty little laces turn any pair of running shoes into slip-ons, perfect for a speedy bike-run transition, and their elasticity keeps your shoes secure. The original 48-inch laces come in 13 different colors because we know: Aesthetics matter on race day.

Yes, we know this little multi-purpose towel was designed for backpacking and camping, but its super-absorbent design can come in very handy for triathletes – whether to dry your feet in T1, wipe down your bike after a sweaty indoor training session, or dry off or wipe down gear after a swim workout. It comes in a small carry pouch with a mini carabiner, so you can clip it to your swim bag or transition bag for easy access.

Keep goggles fog-free with this 2-ounce, easy-to-apply solution (and it’s a big upgrade from using your own saliva!). The formula is environmentally friendly and dries quickly.

Adjust your handlebar, stem, saddle, disc brakes, and seat post (and more!) with the hex wrenches, hex socket, and flathead screwdriver that all fit into this compact, 110-gram multi-tool from a well-established cycling tool brand.

Experience the wonder of toe socks with this low-profile Injinji pair – their signature five-toe design prevents blisters and allows your toes to splay naturally when running. They’re made from sweat-wicking fibers and post-consumer recycled polyester.

Keep your tire repair kit as lightweight as possible with this mini inflator head, possibly the smallest on the market. It uses a twist-style design – no trigger or pump action – that can simply be threaded and then unthreaded to start the flow of CO2.

Get on-the-go injury self-treatment with this 3-inch rubber spiky massage ball that provides deep-tissue relief. It’s especially effective for plantar fasciitis.

Make any post-sunset workout safer with these versatile flashing LED reflectors. It uses a dual magnet to attach to shorts, waistband, caps, hydration belt, or sleeves, and it weighs less than half an ounce, so you won’t even feel it.

#8818. Your 2027 Gravel Calendar Starts Here: 5 Events Worth Planning Your Season Around

Five standout gravel events with epic routes, big vibes, and reasons to train all winter.

On a recent gravel ride one of my riding buddies was telling me that he is beginning to feel like he is falling into a rut with his riding. It’s the same ride from his house during the week and the same group ride on the weekends. I told him that one of my favorite ways to get out of a rut is to sign up for an event. With so many events out there it can be hard to figure out which one to pick.

Gravel has been a growing category for years and looking through the gravel events around the US can feel like you are falling into a doom scroll. When figuring out which one to pick it can be overwhelming because there are so many grinders, group rides, and gravel fondos to choose from.

Signing up for an event a few months out can help get you out of a rut by giving you a goal to strive for. Maybe you add strength training over the winter or maybe you do those zone two rides you ignore. Either way finding the right event can reinvigorate your stoke for riding, especially rolling into the winter.

We gathered a small list of rides from around the country to make it easier for you to set up your gravel calendar for 2027. Whether you want to ride in the mountains of Colorado or the plains of Kansas we have a route for you.

Note: Gravel is ever-growing and changing. As such, entry fees and festivities can change year to year. You can generally expect some free schwag like socks, a tee, or a hat with your entry fee, as well as complimentary food, beverages, and event celebrations. Some events are also affiliated with charities and donate a portion of the entry fee to those causes.

Held during late winter deep in the red-dirt country, The Mid South is a tough challenge to prepare for. It could be a sunny, warm, beautifully leg-searing ripping fast day or a freezing, rainy, slick, sticky, gloppy death march for 100 miles. It all depends on what mother nature has in store. As one of the iconic events on the gravel calendar, it attracts a deep field of pros and recreational riders looking to test their fitness and tune-up for the season ahead. Rain or shine, riders are rewarded with a huge, welcoming community in downtown Stillwater, shared camaraderie with more than 3,600 registrants, and finish line hugs from the event’s passionate and animated promotor Bobby Wintle.

This amalgamation of a gravel grinder meets enduro features nearly 60 miles and 8,000 feet of elevation over gravel roads and sometimes sketchy singletrack trails. The organizers crown the winner based on performance on a handful of shorter, timed segments within the ride. So, you can stop and Instagram the massive views of Mt. Shasta and the Eddy Mountain Range and enjoy all the food and beverages at the aid stations. Though this is billed as a gravel race, the course goes through the Gateway Trail network—a popular mountain biking destination in the area—so you’ll find yourself on singletrack with berms and slightly techy rock gardens. This event is for you if you love ripping singletrack on drop-bar bikes.

Note: Grinduro has expanded to other locations around the world, including Wales, the U.K., Italy, Switzerland, Japan, and Australia.

Known as the Super Bowl of gravel, the 200-mile Unbound (formerly DK200) event is undoubtedly the granddaddy of the gravel scene. Its reputation for being brutal is well earned. The Flint Hills are endlessly rolling and covered in sharp, often chunky gravel. It can be extremely windy, stiflingly hot, and covered in sticky peanut butter mud. It is a badge of honor to finish this sinister double century before the 3 a.m. cut-off time.

There’s a lottery to get in due to the popularity of the event and it just opened up. Throw your name in that hat now with drawings to be announced on November 21. With the entire town joining in the celebration of gravel, it’s something to behold.

You’ll find a star-studded deep pro field leading the charge of this challenging high-altitude course, as one of the hallmarks of the race is generous and equal payouts for men and women. The 108-mile main event Black course features 8,189 feet of climbing. The sweeping vistas of the surrounding mountain ranges, lakes, and ranches take the sting out of the long, exposed climbs. The terrain ranges from fast hard pack to soft, sketchy moon dust, and it includes one long, chunky road right at the end. Steamboat is located at 6,900 feet of altitude, and the course tops out at about 8,200, which riders from sea level will undoubtedly feel.

This event in the northern area of Pennsylvania doesn’t have the alpine views of Steamboat or the prestige of Unbound. What it does have is exactly what the name implies—seemingly endless climbing. This year I completed the 115 mile route and I was impressed that we were on very small bits of paved road throughout the over one hundred mile course. When I talked to the organizer, David Landis, after the race he said the area has even more gravel than he can include into any of these loops.

One tip if you are going to go for any of these distances—bring your climbing legs. Whether you choose the 115 or the 430 mile routes you’ll be getting close to the golden ratio of climbing to miles. If you sign up for the race you need a GPS device (like a Garmin InReach) that can be used to live track the ride.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.
