#8787. Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

Your power meter might be working perfectly, but that doesn’t mean your cycling computer records data accurately. Here’s why you should care and how you can check.

Spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll quickly learn that they don’t always agree. Put a power meter on your crank and another on your pedals, and the numbers may not match exactly. That can be frustrating when you’re trying to figure out which one is right, but for most riders, a small, consistent difference isn’t necessarily a problem.

If you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month. Whether your threshold is actually 250 watts or 255 watts matters less than knowing that an interval at that power represents the same effort from one ride to the next.

But what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers? What if the bike computer recording your ride is changing the data before you ever upload it to Strava or TrainingPeaks?

I recently noticed something odd while testing a cycling computer. At first, I was doing this to compare GPS track accuracy, but since I was testing, I also paired all the devices to my heart rate strap and Quarq power meter. When I compared the ride files afterward, what stood out was that their power numbers didn’t match. Initially, the differences were small enough. But when I looked more closely, I noticed it immediately. Every time I stopped pedaling, one computer still recorded power.

Before I get into what the heck sticky watts are, I should say I first learned about the issue in 2025 when I saw a video from Shane Miller, who goes by GPLama on YouTube. The video is called “Power Meter Data Recording: The Wild West?”, and it’s worth watching. Shane was the first person I saw digging into this particular recording issue with cycling computers.

So what the heck is it? Sticky watts happen when a cycling computer keeps recording a power value for a few seconds after you’ve stopped pedaling. Instead of dropping to zero, the last power number gets “stuck” in your ride file until the computer finally catches up.

Let’s say you’re riding along at 250 watts and stop pedaling as you approach a corner. Your computer might continue recording 250 watts for a few seconds while you’re coasting. On a graph, that can look like a flat line extending beyond the point where the power should have dropped.

A few seconds might not sound like much, but think about how often you stop pedaling on a typical ride. Every corner, descent, stop sign, or moment spent coasting in the group is another opportunity for those extra watts to show up in your file. And if you stop pedaling after a hard effort, the computer could be holding a much higher number than 250 watts, which can skew your data.

It’s also worth distinguishing this from the setting on some computers that lets you exclude zeroes when calculating average power. That setting changes how an average is calculated. Sticky watts affect the power values recorded in the ride file itself, so those extra values can still be there when you upload the ride for analysis.

On one ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Garmin Edge 850 and an Edge 1060. The two Garmins recorded almost identical power numbers, but the DURA 2 consistently came out higher. When I looked more closely at the files, I found repeated instances where the COROS continued recording the last power value after both Garmins had dropped to zero.

The difference was especially noticeable during a series of short, hard efforts. After one effort, the DURA 2 recorded 565 watts for four seconds while both Garmins recorded zero. After another, it held 656 watts for three seconds. Across a roughly three-minute section containing several of these efforts, the Garmins averaged about 260 watts, while the COROS recorded nearly 307 watts.

Those short efforts make the issue easy to see, but the difference showed up across the ride, too. In the roughly 98 minutes of matched power data I compared, the DURA 2 averaged about 186 watts, while both Garmins averaged about 179 watts.

On a second ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Hammerhead Karoo, Wahoo ELEMNT ACE, and Garmin Edge 850. Again, the COROS recorded higher power through a section with several hard efforts followed by coasting. The Garmin recorded lower numbers than the Karoo and Wahoo in that section, which reminds us that differences can go both ways when computers record the same power meter.

I was honestly surprised to see this on the DURA 2. The original DURA had similar issues early on, but its power recording improved with subsequent updates, and it performed well in GPLama’s 2025 video presenting the issue. I don’t want to turn this into a story about picking on COROS. The company has a good history of updating and improving its products, and I expect it can address this issue on the DURA 2 as well. For now, these files show why it’s worth paying attention to what your cycling computer records, even when you trust your power meter.

If you mostly ride for fun and don’t pay much attention to your power data afterward, a few extra watts in your ride file probably won’t change your life. But if you use that data to track your training, compare rides, and work with a coach, those differences can matter.

The big problem is that sticky watts don’t necessarily add the same amount to every ride. A steady climb with little coasting might show no difference. But a ride with lots of corners, stop signs, descents, or short, hard efforts followed by coasting could produce a much larger one. That makes it harder to compare rides or judge how much work you actually did.

The easiest way to check is to record the same ride on two cycling computers paired to the same power meter. You don’t necessarily need to buy a second computer. If a friend has one you can borrow, pair both to your power meter and record a ride with a few clear transitions from pedaling to coasting.

Alternatively, you can look closely at the power files your head unit generates. Do a couple of hard efforts, like sprints, where you stop pedaling at the end, then zoom in on those sections. Look for a flat section where one computer continues recording the same power value for several seconds after the other has dropped to zero.

And yes, I know that I’m definitely in some deep weeds over here, and it can be tough to argue that a cycling computer recording a few extra watts is a huge problem worth tackling. For many riders, it might not matter at all. But the current crop of cycling computers is also the most expensive we’ve ever seen. These devices are marketed and sold as precision training tools, and accurate data recording is central to that. These devices should do that, and riders shouldn’t have to question it.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. #8785. Nike’s Goal With the Structure Plus? Make Stability Less Boring

The brand’s classic stability shoe gets the super trainer treatment with a tall stack height, lighter weight, and PEBA added to the midsole.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

How do you change runners’ conception about stability? Last December at The Running Event in San Antonio, Texas, Nike Expert PLM Ashley Campbell held up the answer: the Structure Plus.

“Stability can be boring,” she admitted. The Structure Plus makes it exciting.

The shoe follows the Vomero Plus, a super trainer version of the Vomero 18. The Structure Plus is the super-ified version of the Structure 26. Where the latter is more accessible for $140, the “plus” iteration is the original amplified in every aspect.

The Structure Plus became my chosen shoe for long runs during my 2026 Boston Marathon training cycle. Here’s how the shoe won me over on a 12-miler, and why you should consider trying a stability super trainer.

While developing the Structure Plus, Campbell said the team set out to make the super trainer “more supportive, smoother, softer, and more palatable.”

Tech-wise, you can see how Nike landed on the first three. The shoe’s platform is wider to provide support. A convex flat shape of sidewall provides stability, the density underneath the arch acting as a stabilizer to help with alignment. A dual layer of foams, like in the Vomero Plus, provides a soft, energizing ride.

In terms of making the shoe more palatable, Campbell wanted the Structure Plus to be all-inclusive. “You don’t have to be an overpronator [to run in the shoe.]”

At 42 mm in the heel and 32 mm in the forefoot, it’d make sense if you expected the shoe to be heavy and unstable. But the Structure Plus challenges these notions.

At 10.9 ounces, men’s 10, the shoe is lighter than the Structure 26, which weighs 11.3 ounces. The maximal cushioning is a layer of PEBA-based ZoomX, a soft foam that delivers high rebound (the foam is also in Nike’s premium marathon shoe, the Alphafly), and TPE-based ReactX, a firmer foam that helps stabilize your ride (the same foam found in the Vomero 18).

Despite the high stack height and max cushioning and stability components, the shoe didn’t weigh me down on my runs, nor did it cause my feet to roll. I didn’t feel like I was forced into alignment. The shoes guide you instead of directing your foot.

It was such a contrast after running in the Vomero Plus the weekend before. During those miles, it got to the point where my friends were getting concerned after I tripped over myself for the umpteenth time. My next long run was smooth, all thanks to the Structure Plus for keeping me stable.

I’m a neutral runner, but as the miles pile on, like they do on long runs, my form gets erratic due to fatigue. It’s those later miles where the Structure Plus saves me from hitting the pavement, or worse, benching myself with injury.

Concerning actual overpronators, our testers were satisfied with the support the shoe provided.

“What I liked most about the Nike Structure Plus was the strong sense of support it delivered on every run,” said tester and overpronator Julian Caiazzo. “The shoe felt stable and dependable without ever coming across as stiff or restrictive. It gave me the confidence to settle into my stride, and even with all that structure, the ride still felt smooth and enjoyable.”

Another overpronator, Katherine Thomas, admitted she usually avoids Nike shoes because of their lack of stability. She was pleasantly surprised with the support of the Structure Plus.

If there’s any reason why you should try the Structure Plus, it isn’t just that it’ll change your preconceived notion of a stability shoe; it’ll also change what you think of Nike trainers.

Like Thomas, I also avoided Nike shoes (unless I had to test them) because of their lack of stability and narrow fit. The Structure Plus doesn’t feel like a Nike shoe; there’s no squeezing on the sides of my midfoot, no pinching by my toes. And yet, I reap that quintessential Nike ride, that layer of ZoomX adding more pop to my strides. Those long runs are anything but boring slogs. I can emphatically say that Nike achieved its goal of making stability—and my runs—more exciting.

#8784. The Best Advanced GPS Running Watches of 2026, Tested by an Ultrarunner

I tested these premium running watches on city streets, mountain trails, and at ultra distances to find out which features are worth paying for.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

I review a ton of running watches, cycling through all of the various features and idiosyncrasies to find which watch would suit which runner best, which watches deserve a place on our lists, and which don’t measure up. Sometimes, there are watches that are really cool, and do a lot of work, but they offer more than what the average runner needs to log their daily miles and monitor their fitness. But for backwoods adventure runners, ultrarunners, or runners who put a lot of demand on their machines, advanced GPS running watches like the ones on this list offer a bit more of everything—from cellular and satellite connectivity to off-road trail mapping to sturdier cases, more multisport functionality, and all around just more.

As an ultrarunner, I am frequently testing watches for 50, 75, or even 100 miles at a stretch. Often these miles are spent deep in the woods in Upstate New York on trails that are poorly marked and pretty treacherous. Sometimes, there simply isn’t cell service to be had—anywhere. On top of that, I routinely test them during Hyrox, kayaking, paddle boarding, weight training, hiking, and even skiing—when there’s actually snow on the ground. My daily runs tend toward miles spent in New York City, which you wouldn’t think is an issue, but the tall buildings can thwart GPS pretty hard.

Looking for more running tech? Read our reviews of the best wireless headphones for running, headlamps for runners, and basic running watches.

The Fenix 9 is not flawless, but dang, it is as close to it as I’ve ever tested.I’ve put over 300 miles on the Pro Solar, so I’ll get my little nitpicks out of the way first. Annoyingly, there’s a lag of about half a second to a second when you start a workout, and again when you switch between laps that the 8 did not have. It’s not the most annoying thing in the world, but alas. Also, the app is still the Garmin Connect app. (I will beat this drum until they fix it.)

Now? My happy place, the good stuff. The solar ring on the Pro Solar model puts this watch so far ahead of every other run watch on the market that it can’t even see the others from the rearview. The 51mm is rated for up to 57 days in smartwatch mode with solar, and the 47mm gets up to 34. In the 51mm’s max battery GPS mode, that stretches to 186 hours, or up to 1,000 with solar. I took this out in the backwoodsiest of backwoods Adirondack trails, where I forced it to rely wholly on satellite, and I ran it for 12 solid hours, and it barely ticked the battery.

And that multiband GPS with SatIQ? It’s the best in class, and it locks you down in a hurry. The inReach satellite connectivity lets me run those backwoods and feel safe about doing so. (Though, I still bring a SatCom.)

It’s built like a beast without feeling like one. This is the first Fenix with a titanium case, plus a sapphire lens and a 10 ATM water rating, so rain, sweat, and my early morning postrun ocean swims don’t screw it up.

It’s chockablock with performance and training metrics, and with Epic, their new multiday activity tracker, it’s better than ever. It’s light on the wrist, and it’s easy to use even with sweaty or sea salty fingers.

My favorite little bonus is the flashlight. It’s dimmable and comes in white, red, or green, so it’s great for visibility on early morning runs and also for finding crap at the bottom of my purse.

The base Fenix 9 is a solid watch too, but the Pro Solar is the one I’d get. It’s simply a very fine watch.

You might not be familiar with this brand, but when I tell you, they are punching so far above their weight class with this watch that you would think a 10-year-old just knocked out Floyd Mayweather, I’m not kidding.

The Amazfit Balance Ultra costs $599.99. For that you get a Grade 5 titanium case, a sapphire lens, and a 10 ATM rating that also covers freediving and recreational scuba. It weighs 57 grams without the strap, which is a lot of watch for so little weight. It’s a bit on the thicker side, but not so high profile it’s going to get caught on doors.

Battery is where things start to get unbelievable. The 780 mAh cell battery is rated for up to 30 days of typical use and 10 with the always-on display. In accurate GPS mode you get 50 hours, and power-saving GPS stretches to about 90 in our testing. Unless you’re running through the weekend, you’ll hit your limit before the watch does.

For tracking, it uses dual-band GPS across six satellite systems that ends up acting just like a typical multiband GPS on par with a Coros or a Suunto. That is clutch when you run between tall buildings or under tree cover and your watch would otherwise decide you swam across the Hudson. The 1.5-inch AMOLED screen is bright enough that it can be read in direct sun for the most part.

I will say that the dang buttons on the side are far too easy to depress, leading to accidentally starting activities, but overall, it’s incredible.

The Garmin Enduro 4 is a light upgrade from the 3. It has increased storage, an upgraded band, and introduces some more in-built activities like rucking and rowing alongside Garmin’s multiday training tool Epic. The Enduro line is built for multi-day trekking. Everything about it is engineered for endurance—the rugged design, precise tracking, and especially the solar-powered battery that seems to last forever. You don’t even think about charging most days; it just handles your training, races, and long trail days without missing a beat. The safety and satellite coverage give you extra peace of mind when you’re out alone, far from cell service or the nearest trailhead.

Two features stand out on every serious run. The Pack Weight tool adjusts your effort estimates based on how heavy your gear is, which makes your performance data feel more real—especially on long mountain efforts. And the Next Fork guide keeps you on track, showing how far it is to the next junction so that you don’t have to stop and fumble through maps. Add Garmin’s multiband GPS with SatiQ tech that automatically switches between the best systems into the mix, and logs routes that are spot-on, no matter how deep into the woods you go.

For ultrarunners or anyone training big, the Enduro 4 is reliability wrapped around your wrist—with battery life that feels almost unfair.

I’ve been using the Suunto Vertical 2 off and on for a while now, and I’ve come to see it as a true multisport powerhouse rather than an everyday watch. It’s the one I pull out when training or adventures get serious—long runs, big mountain weekends, or backcountry routes where accuracy and endurance matter more than aesthetics. What sets it apart immediately are its maps—they’re crisp, easy to read, and fully offline, which makes navigation seamless even in the most remote terrain.

Battery life is another standout feature. The Vertical 2 easily lasts up to 60 days in smartwatch mode and delivers exceptional runtime with dual-band GNSS tracking, something that still amazes me every time I scroll through my recorded routes after multihour training blocks. The titanium and sapphire glass construction give it a premium, expedition-ready feel, and the watch itself feels built to handle harsh conditions without flinching.

It’s definitely not what I’d wear every day—it’s large, rugged, and purpose-built—but that’s exactly the point. For athletes who bounce between cycling, running, skiing, hiking, and more, the Vertical 2 is a multisport dream, offering a level of mapping, tracking, and battery endurance suited for endless exploration.

The Garmin Forerunner 970 has been my daily watch for months, and it feels like the perfect blend of lifestyle usability and serious athletic performance. It’s light, comfortable, and sleek enough to wear all day—but underneath that understated design is a fully loaded training tool built for racing, coaching, and multidiscipline endurance work. Whether I’m tracking an interval session, planning an ultra-block, or guiding athletes through structured workouts, the 970 handles it all seamlessly.

GPS precision is exceptional thanks to its multiband GNSS system, locking on quickly and maintaining accuracy even through tree cover and narrow streets. The built-in coaching and training readiness tools have become part of my daily routine—providing recovery insights, suggested sessions, and race forecasts that actually feel tailored. For multisport training, it transitions modes smoothly, syncing effortlessly with sensors and Garmin Connect data.

As someone who loves to spend their hard-earned money on running in a pack of fellow weirdos at races, the pace predictor and race features are a big draw for the Garmin Forerunner 970. I sync my races from Garmin Connect, and the watch spits out predicted times for 5K up to marathons based on my VO2 max, training load, and recent runs, updating as I log more miles. What seals it for me are the race markers overlaid on the course profile, showing projected splits and elevation-adjusted pacing so I can visualize where to surge or conserve energy without second-guessing midrace. It's like having a personal coach whispering realistic goal times right before the gun goes off, turning pricey pack running into a heart-thumping hunt for a PR.

Battery life remains solid, though not as extreme as Garmin’s solar or expedition-focused models, lasting up to 20 days in smartwatch mode. Add in smart notifications, music storage, contactless payments, and wrist-based navigation, and it becomes a rare hybrid—a true performance watch that fits effortlessly into everyday life.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a vast improvement over the Ultra 3, which is a polite way of saying the Ultra 3 had room to grow.

GPS now locks on fast. Apple says there’s no change here, but other members of my team and I noticed a difference. It might be in the software updates, but it’s better. I'm no longer starting runs before the watch has made up its mind. Once it has locked on, though, it commits to a story that isn’t quite true. Distance runs consistently one to one and a half percent long. During a marathon, that’s a few tenths of a mile I didn't earn.

Battery, thankfully, is finally impressing me. It’s leaps and bounds better, and it charges absurdly fast. I top it up while the coffee brews and I take my shower, and by the time I’m done, it’s fully loaded and ready to go.

Heart rate is the big jump. Against a Holter monitor, it stayed within two to three bpm on steady efforts. Run hard and it drifts to five to seven. I do wish it sampled my heart rate every second of every day instead of every five, but overall I don’t think the difference is huge, and when you combine that with the beauty of their apps, it’s hardly a thing.

What’s missing for me is lactate threshold. I can live without many advanced run metrics, but I like knowing my threshold for training runs.

In their new and improved health app, the ECG and hypertension alerts are useful, the cycle insights are spot on, and the morning report doesn’t make me feel graded. Transit pay, apps, and phone integration are unmatched. Satellite calling is extremely easy compared to any other watch I’ve tried. It’s a freaking great watch, overall.

When you step into the world of high-end GPS running watches, the sheer number of options can feel overwhelming—until you see the immense power packed into these bad boys. The essentials are non-negotiable: rock-solid multiband GPS precision, exceptional battery life (no one wants to lose tracking on a 50K run), accurate heart rate and recovery metrics, and seamless integration with your training plans. Every watch on this list delivers on those core requirements.

Where they start to spread their wings is everything layered on top. The bells and whistles are kinda wild. Things like dual-frequency GPS for navigating deep woods (or mountaintops), topo and trail maps that actually make sense when you’re lost, and multisport modes that keep up whether you’re running, swimming, skiing, triathlon training, or rolling through a Hyrox circuit. Barometric altitude readings, pulse ox sensors, and training readiness scores just round out the “how cooked am I?” data we’ve all come to both love and loathe in equal measure.

Some watches, though, don’t just tell you about your fitness—they could save your butt in a sticky situation. The Garmin Fenix 8 Pro works with Garmin’s inReach satellite system, letting you text or send an SOS nowhere near cell service. The Apple Watch Ultra takes a slightly different route with built-in satellite SOS and cellular, so if you’re off-grid and something goes sideways, you’re not shouting into the void. These are the kinds of features that make the difference between just tracking a run and actually trusting your gear if things go sideways.

Let’s be honest—most runners don’t need a watch this powerful. But if you’re out there chasing hours instead of miles, exploring trail networks that don’t even show up on Google Maps, or toggling between swim intervals, mountain climbs, and winter ski sessions, these make a world of difference. Basically, if you’re a runner like me with electricity in your veins and the ADHD that drives you toward multisport or off-the-beaten-trail running, these watches are for you.

One of the quietest but most important reasons these watches shine is safety. With incident detection, live tracking, fall alerts, and SOS tools that actually connect you to help, they turn your wrist into a mini rescue hub. The Garmins can ping your emergency contacts automatically or connect through inReach. The Apple Watch Ultra fires off emergency signals via satellite if you end up out of range. And even the Suunto Vertical and Coros Vertix 2S earn their stripes here with detailed offline maps and batteries that cruise through multi-day efforts.

Basically, these aren’t just training tools—they’re peace of mind on your wrist. When you’re 10 miles deep in a trail system and the forest gets quiet, it’s nice knowing your watch is smarter about directions and safety than your phone or maybe even you.

The Aventon Level is our benchmark electric bike. It’s a great e-bike for commuting, running errands, or leisure riding. The Level platform has proven to be reliable, low-maintenance, and fun to ride—and it doesn’t break the bank.

Riders will also find the Level’s connected features very useful. The Level 4’s ACU (Aventon Control Unit) adds several smart features to the already well-equipped platform. The wheel lock and motion sensor alarm are passive theft deterrents when you stop for a mid-ride coffee or run into the post office. A 4G chip in the ACU enables GPS tracking in Aventon’s mobile app, so you can locate your bike if you forget where you locked it. 4G connectivity also allows you to set geofence restrictions on the bike for teens or housemates.

Compared with earlier Aventure versions, the third-generation model rides smoother and feels more like a premium bike (without the high price tag). Aventon’s new torque sensor allows more control over the acceleration of Aventure’s 750W rear hub motor. Lighter-weight testers found previous models had too much torque, but Aventure fixed that issue. Additional features include a new head-unit interface, integrated turn signals, a front light, a rear rack, and fenders.

The Aventure 3 is an excellent fat-tire e-bike for commuters—especially on snowy days and gravel paths. Off-road, it excels on doubletrack trails and cinder paths. However, the bike is burly; its weight and components limit its fun on technical singletrack and more aggressive mountain trails.

Aventon also offers a mid-drive version of the Aventure. It keeps the same big, burly character but adds a more premium feel, a smoother, more powerful motor, and an upgraded drivetrain—along with a higher price.

Aventon’s Pace 5 REC is a zippy e-bike that’s perfect for weekend cruises around town, the bike path, or even occasional commutes. The brand refined the Pace with a slew of updates, making it one of the best bang-for-your-buck step-throughs on the market. These include connected features (such as GPS tracking and theft deterrence), a powerful 750 Watt motor, regenerative braking, and an impressive 75-mile range. It’s offered in five colors (grey, mint, pink, orange, and teal) and two frame sizes.

The Pace 5 does not come with a rack, fenders, or a suspension fork. If you commute by bike frequently or use your e-bike for running errands, consider paying $200 more for the Level 4.

Buying an e-bike on Amazon can be risky, especially if you don’t know much about bikes or have much mechanical experience. However, sometimes you can find a good deal on a decent bike. At $500, the Heybike Cityscape isn’t the pinnacle of e-bike tech, but it helps you get out and enjoy some rides without busting your budget.

The Cityscape stands out for its combination of low price, practical features (like a rack and fenders), and a UL-certified battery. Unlike some Amazon brands, Heybike offers a U.S. support line for warranty service or product questions.

Includes FREE accessories: Fast Charger, Running Boards, Frame Bag, Cushions, Elite Headlight, Seatpost, Comfort Seat, and Orbitor.

Many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. Discounted to $1,699, the dual-battery model has up to 120 miles of range and a 28 mph top speed. A single-battery version is also available for $1,399; it boasts an impressive 60-mile range. Need even more battery power? The $1,999 Long Range model goes up to 170 miles from a single charge.

These prices make the XPedition one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes on the market. And they’re a solid option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike. “The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, said Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers and the Essentials package, I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”

Includes FREE accessories: Rear Rack, Water-Resistant Panniers, Lock, Elite Headlight, Seatpost, Comfort Saddle, Phone Mount, and Mirrors.

If you want power and range in a small package, the XP4 750 is right for you. It’s a fast, zippy Class 3 e-bike (pedal assist up to 28 mph) with a 330-pound payload capacity. To increase the XP4’s function and fun, the 750 has a 1310-watt peak motor output (200 watts more than the standard model) and an 85-mile range.

Whether you’re riding city streets on your commute or out for a weekend ride, this bike is fast, easy to ride, and a blast to pedal.

Includes FREE accessories: Rear Rack, Fenders, Headlight, and Seatpost.

The XP Lite 2.0 scales back the XP4 750’s top speed and power, with pedal assist topping out at 20 mph, a peak motor output of 819 watts, and a reduced payload capacity of 275 pounds. It also drops the suspension fork found on the XP4, but still delivers an impressive range of up to 80 miles.

However, the XP Lite isn’t simply a stripped-down version of the XP4; it has some major advantages. At 49 pounds (without accessories and options), it’s 26 pounds lighter than the higher-powered model. This makes the Lite much easier to lift and transport. Plus, instead of an 8-speed drivetrain, the XP Lite features a low-maintenance Gates belt drive. That means no greasy chain, no finicky gear adjustments, and a quieter, cleaner ride. Yes, it’s a singlespeed, but the pedal-assist motor easily compensates for all but the steepest hills or heaviest loads.

Includes FREE accessories: Support Seat, Elite Headlight, Suspension Seatpost, and Cargo Package.

Electric trikes are a great choice for many riders, including seniors, people with mobility limitations, and those who need to carry heavy payloads. At $1,699, the Lectric XP Trike2 is an easy-to-ride, stable three-wheeler.

A 750-watt motor with 1,310 peak watts powers the XP Trike up to 17 mph and up to 70 miles of range on a charge. The Trike features a wide, soft seat with back support. Plus, it has a suspension seatpost and suspension fork for added comfort.

With a top speed of 28 mph, 81 miles of range, a 100mm-travel suspension fork, 27.5”x2.6”, a rack, and fenders, the Adventure Neo Allroad Speed’s name fits it to a T. This bike is built for adventures large and small, from commutes to work in the snow or rain, to gravel trails at your local park.

To power the Adventure, Cannondale uses a Bafang 750W rear hub motor and an easy-access 750 Wh removable battery. With its power and wide-range 8-speed drivetrain, you will get up every hill, while Tektro hydraulic disc brakes will control your speed on descents. Plus, it’s available in flashy red or more subdued matte black.

At $1,200, this Cannondale is 45% off its original price and is equipped with better parts than many lesser-known brands’ bikes priced hundreds more.

Many “step-through” e-bikes lack a truly low-step design, making them difficult for some riders to mount or dismount. However, the CTY e2.1, from REI’s Co-op house brand, has a fully step-through front triangle. This makes the CTY a great choice for older riders, those with mobility limitations, or others who seek an easy-to-ride e-bike.

REI equips the CTY e2.1 with a 250-watt hub-drive motor; it provides smooth pedal assistance up to 20 mph. It also features a suspension fork to smooth out bumps and potholes, an adjustable stem to custom-tune your riding position, and hydraulic disc brakes for improved stopping power. For less than the cost of many unknown e-bikes online, you can get a quality electric bike backed up by REI’s warranty and service.

Salsa’s Moraine 145 costs less than many hardtail E-MTBs. But don’t let the price fool you; this bike is value-packed. This dual 29-inch-wheeled trail bike comes equipped with Fazua’s Ride 60 motor (60 Newton-meters of torque) and a 430-Watt-hour battery. While it has less torque and a smaller-capacity battery than higher-priced competitors, it has enough power for some serious fun in the woods and on singletrack.

The frame uses a Split Pivot suspension system designed by Dave Weagle (the mastermind behind the dw-link suspension system on Pivot bikes), for a balance of performance and pedalability. A 10-speed Shimano Cues drivetrain, four-piston Shimano brakes, a dropper post, and Terravail tubeless tires round out the components of this feature-packed full-suspension E-MTB.

Electric bikes are great for commuting and city life. However, their added weight (sometimes as much as 90 or 100 pounds) can make e-bikes a pain to carry up flights of stairs, load onto a bus or train, or even move around in your garage.

Weighing only about 40 pounds, the Roadster v3 cuts weight without sacrificing much performance or adding cost. Ride1Up uses a 500 watt/50Nm rear hub motor with an internal battery for a clean, stealthy look. 700x45c gravel tires carry speed on pavement or hardpack dirt roads, and metal fenders keep the road spray off your clothes.

Electric mountain bikes are a ton of fun and help you ride more of your favorite trails. We recommend full-suspension E-MTBs for aggressive and technical trails. But hardtails often work fine on easier trails and mellower terrain, and they cost a lot less than dual-suspension models.

Velotric keeps costs low on the Summit 1 by using a rear hub motor instead of a pricier mid-drive unit. The Summit also features an 8-speed Shimano drivetrain rather than more expensive 11- or 12-speed systems. However, Velotric gives the bike a 120mm thru-axle fork to soak up bumps, Shimano hydraulic disc brakes, and a full-color screen with Bluetooth connectivity.

Electric bikes are a great way for older riders to enjoy cycling and stay active. However, many commuter e-bikes have high top tubes, and even many step-through-style frames still require riders to swing their leg over the frame. The Velotric Discover has a Euro-style, low-step-through frame that makes it easier to get on and off.

Additional comfort features include an adjustable-rise stem, wide seat, and suspension seatpost. The Discover has a 28mph top speed and about 75 miles of range. At 63 pounds, it’s not super light, but it weighs less than many similarly priced e-bikes.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8782. 7 Common 5K Training Mistakes Runners Make

Everything you should avoid for a faster 3.1 miles.

The 5K is a staple in many runners’ racing schedules, and training for one comes with its own unique strategies for interval workouts, long runs, nutrition, and recovery. All of these factors are bound to leave room for error, so you’ll likely run into some pitfalls as you prep for 3.1 miles.

Some common missteps runners face might even lead to injury, explains Maya Ellison, C.P.T., RRCA-certified run coach and owner of P.A.C.E.D. Coaching Services. If you don’t optimize your training method, you’re also likely to keep getting the same results, which may not lead to that PR you’re vying to achieve, she says. Even if you’re a seasoned runner with dozens of 5Ks under your belt, there’s always room for improvement. “Doing it before doesn’t make you an expert,” says Ellison.

So you can surely take a couple notes from run coaches in order to run your best 5K yet. To better prepare for all your favorite seasonal 3.1-milers and help you feel confident at the start line, we spoke with run coaches to unpack the most common mistakes runners make when training for a 5K.

For many runners, 5Ks are easier to jump into compared to a marathon, which requires a solid block of training time to adjust to high mileage and fueling demands. With a 5K, you might tag along at a friend’s race or sign up last minute. Because of this, you might squeeze in a bunch of speed workouts within a few weeks before the race, which can leave you feeling tired or flat come race day, says Sam Renikoff, USATF- and RRCA-certified run coach.

While you can get away with a shorter training block for a 5K, it’s still important to give yourself enough time to absorb your training, recover, and feel 100 percent going into the race, Renikoff explains. For example, rather than tapering for three weeks before race day like you would training for a marathon, Renikoff recommends tapering for a week to 10 days before a 5K, keeping intensity high with speedwork but cutting back on volume.

Plus, going from zero to 100 can lead to getting sidelined, according to Debbie Woodruff, USATF- and RRCA-certified run coach and certified personal trainer. That’s because runners who increase mileage too quickly—rather than taking small steps toward more volume—are more likely to face injury, according to a study published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine.

To mitigate the risk, Woodruff recommends beginners follow a couch-to-5K plan or a run/walk training plan to ease into training with a gradual buildup, while more seasoned runners should follow an eight-week-long plan that also allows you to build mileage, add speedwork, and prioritize the prerace taper.

Sticking to an expert-backed training plan, like Runner’s World’s 5K training plans, allows you to have structure and give yourself time to adjust to the demands of the distance.

Renikoff explains that even though 5Ks are much shorter than a marathon or half, the long run is still crucial. It allows you to get comfortable with being uncomfortable, an important part of the 5K. It also prevents you from giving into fatigue by building your endurance, which allows you to hold onto your pace through the entire 3.1 miles. Plus, the long run often acts as a confidence booster, making the 5K less intimidating all around.

The long run is one of the best ways to increase your aerobic capacity, Renikoff explains. This is important even for shorter race distances because you need to use oxygen to efficiently produce energy for any run lasting longer than just a few minutes.

Long runs during 5K training will typically range anywhere from 4.5 miles (for more beginners) to 12 miles (for advanced runners with time-based goals like breaking 20 minutes). That means some plans may triple the distance of your race, which will only make you more prepared to conquer 3.1 miles.

Seasoned runners in particular might struggle to keep their easy runs easy, Ellison explains, because of their experience, fitness levels, or overall ambition. But these easy days give your body a chance to recover from hard days, allowing you to get stronger throughout your training cycle, she says.

You should feel relaxed throughout your easy runs, like you’re able to have a conversation with someone. Some runners find it helpful to check in on their effort level with the ABC test: Chant the ABCs out loud and try to get to the letter G without having to take a breath. If you falter, that’s your cue that you need to slow down.

If you make a habit of not taking easy pace seriously, you might even find yourself running a speedy first mile during an easy run or tempo run, only to falter by mile two, progressively getting slower and more fatigued by the end. This happens when runners struggle to find an effective pacing strategy, Renikoff explains.

This makes it more likely you’ll go out too fast on race day, which could sabotage your goals. “If you go out and run the first mile [of the race] 20 seconds faster than your average 5K pace, you’re a lot more likely to have that pace balloon to 30 seconds or more slower [than goal pace] in the second and third miles, which is not only not fun or enjoyable, but it’s also not fast,” Renikoff says.

For smarter pacing, Renikoff suggests progression runs: Start by running the first mile of your tempo run at a moderate pace, then increase your speed each mile or half mile (depending on the distance of your run) by about 10 seconds, finishing significantly faster than you started. This requires you to start slow enough that you can continue to run faster as the workout progresses.

While some runners start their runs too fast, others struggle to run faster than their easy pace at all. “If you’re aiming to run a fast 5K and you have not spent any time in those paces by doing some hard intervals, it’s really easy to give up in the race,” says Renikoff.

The key to not giving up at the first sign of fatigue? Implement one to two days per week of some form of speed training, including intervals and tempo runs, Woodruff says.

Seasoned runners may benefit from track intervals, like 200- to 400-meter repeats at 95-percent effort or goal 5K pace with equal recovery, she explains. Another option is a tempo or threshold run, where you sustain your 5K pace for a prolonged period of time sandwiched by a few easy miles.

A fartlek workout introduces newbie runners to interval training, Woodruff explains, by alternating one to two minutes at a hard effort with one to two minutes at an easy effort, essentially practicing interval training without the need for specific metrics.

If your most recent PR is a 24-minute 5K and you’re trying to run your next one in 19 minutes, you might need to readjust your goal setting, at least for now. Ellison explains that runners sometimes set overly ambitious goals, when in reality, true growth takes time.

Instead of looking to drop five minutes in your next race—which requires you to run nearly two minutes faster per mile—try setting a smaller goal like dropping 30 seconds to one minute from your finish time, Ellison explains. This requires about a 10- to 20-second pace difference per mile, making your PR more manageable to achieve.

A beginner 5K runner may not know how to properly warm up and cool down, explains Ellison, which is especially important for each workout, but also for race day.

Warmups can help you sustain a harder effort for longer periods of time, while cooldowns give your body a chance to actively recover after hard efforts. A solid warmup typically includes dynamic stretching, drills like high knees and butt kicks, along with a five-minute jog, Woodruff explains, while a cooldown should include a mile or two of easy jogging and static stretching.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

#8781. What Top Tri Coaches Fix Between November and March

Top triathlon coaches share what they have their athletes work on in the off-season. (Photo: FinisherPix/Triathlete, Aaron Palaian, Oliver Baker, and courtesy David Tilbury-Davis)

One of triathlon’s attractions – and frustrations – is that there is always something to work on, and there are few better times to continue that never-ending quest for perfection than during the off-season.

With no race commitments, it gives triathletes the opportunity to step back, assess their strengths and weaknesses, and identify what to work on heading into spring.

For Northern Hemisphere athletes, that time is now. So, to help you along the way, we turned to four of the sport’s leading coaches to get their views — in their words — on what triathletes should focus on between now and March.

One of the world’s leading coaches and applied sports scientists in endurance sport, Plews has coached elite triathletes, including world champions Chelsea Sodaro, Javier Gomez, and Terenzo Bozzone.

He is also the founder of the coaching platform Endure IQ for both athletes and coaches. Plews himself is a former age-group Ironman world champion and still holds the fastest amateur time at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship.

“I never did proper strength training when I was younger, but now that I do a lot more, I’m seeing the benefits. But it is only as good as the quality and intent you put in. One of the big mistakes I see with many triathletes is that there’s no real intent.

“Get someone to help make sure you’re doing proper lifts. If you need to learn the correct movements, winter would be an ideal time. Then strength work needs to challenge the system. We typically talk “reps in reserve” when it comes to strength training [i.e., how many more reps you could complete before reaching failure].

“I’d advise working to two to three reps in reserve, but you can go to four if you’re not confident. But the main thing is you want to see a change in the speed of movement as you fatigue through the set.

“I would focus mostly on compound lifts: barbell hip thrusts, Bulgarian split squats, Nordic hamstring curls, and isometric holds and calf raises to add injury prevention. As time goes on, pair it with more plyometric and ballistic exercises, which might be a squat into a box jump.”

“Winter can be a period where you become unstuck from a psychological point of view. What’s important is to find balance. You want the volume, but don’t want to become stale so that by the time you get to the season, you’ve lost enthusiasm.

“If you really push the envelope early, especially with long, cold rides in January and February, by the time you get through to the season, you’re just sick of it. So, I think there’s a very fine line between doing too much training and not enough.”

The founder and head coach of NVDM Coaching in Austin, Texas, Van Der Merwe leads a team of more than 30 coaches supporting over 700 athletes. A former top-50 world-ranked junior tennis player from South Africa, she raced as a professional triathlete from 2010 to 2023 and has coached since 2009. She also leads Ironman U, Ironman’s official coaching certification program.

“Winter is when we raise the ceiling. We reverse periodize, so short, focused threshold and VO2 work comes before the long volume, because every triathlete races at a percentage of their FTP.

“If an athlete raises FTP from 220 to 235 watts this winter and rides an Ironman at 70% of it, race-day power goes from 154 to about 165 watts. Spring then becomes about extending that fitness.”

“Most athletes book a fit in spring, which leaves little time to adapt before racing. Our order is comfort first, then aerodynamics, then power, because the fastest position is the one you can hold for the whole bike leg and still run well afterward.

“In one study, the lowest torso angle tested cost riders about 16 watts at threshold compared with their own positions. Winter trainer rides are the perfect place to build into a new position gradually.”

“This is one most athletes never think about, and it can quietly derail a whole season. Vitamin D drops through the winter, especially for athletes training indoors at northern latitudes.

“A review of more than 2,000 athletes found over half had inadequate levels. Iron stores matter too, especially for female athletes. We ask athletes to get a baseline panel with vitamin D and ferritin now, so their doctor can address anything before the big training blocks start.”

Head coach at KIS Coaching, Cunnama is a former elite professional triathlete from South Africa who won major long-distance races, including Challenge Roth and Ironman Hamburg, and owns two top-five finishes at the Ironman World Championship in Kona. Following his racing career, he became a presenter with the Global Triathlon Network (GTN), sharing his knowledge and experience with a worldwide triathlon audience.

“Everyone knows they should work on their weaknesses over winter, but that usually translates to a broad goal like, ‘I want to work on my swim,’ which then turns into ‘more swimming, less biking and running.’

“I find it more effective to keep a balance in all three triathlon disciplines, but try to get ahead on the things that you always fell behind on last season. Determine which aspect of your training made you feel most underconfident, and then tweak your off-season training to target that area.

“For example, if you found that using paddles destroyed your arms, do extra paddle work. If hills were your nemesis on the bike, hit the hills (or simulate them on the trainer). Rather than tackling physical limitations, target the mental hurdles – use the off-season to get to a place where you love the sessions you hated last season.”

“It is hard to make changes to technique during the season when you have volume goals in training, because technique changes (or position changes on the bike) require you to only do as much of the new technique as you can sustain, and no more.

“You can’t ingrain a new technique when the second half of your session is falling back to the old technique! So, make those changes in the off-season and slowly build back that technique better. The advantage of triathlon is you have two other sports to keep you fit while you reset your technique in the third sport.”

A highly respected triathlon coach, Tilbury-Davis has worked with professional and age-group athletes since 1995. Through Tilbury-Davis Coaching, he has coached leading athletes such as Lionel Sanders and Ashleigh Gentle. Based in Finland, he works with a small group of international athletes.

“Efficiency of movement sounds vague, but while I’m a big proponent of doing strength and conditioning work throughout the year, winter is a time to understand that swimming, biking, and running all require expression of force from the core – when I say core, I effectively mean from the knees to the chest.

“You’re talking around 64 different muscles and creating the capacity to have a stable base to express force from will improve your body alignment in the water, your ability to maintain an aero position on the bike, and your ability to have hip extension and knee drive in the run. It centers around doing the kind of exercises that are multi-plane, multi-muscle recruiting as part of a several-times-a-week program.

“For example, you see a lot of triathletes train with a Masters group and the swim coach says to do a high elbow or chicken wing drill. The reality is that 99% of triathletes do not have sufficient mobility to swim in a manner that a swim coach would like. So, to step back, I would say to improve your swimming, go away and work on your thoracic and scapular mobility.”

“A lot of people don’t talk about saddle choice. We all buy expensive running shoes that are made out of expensive foam that breaks down over a period of time, but we forget that saddles are also made out of foam.

“If you’re serious about maintaining a good position on the bike, you probably should be changing your saddle once a year and for a pro that might be twice a year because the foam in the saddle breaks down the same way that the foam in a running shoe breaks down.”

“Get used to having to cope with uneven surfaces on the run, shortening and lengthening your stride length, stepping over rocks and roots, dealing with off camber, on camber, dealing with gravel, sand, mud, all of those proprioceptive stimuli that vary significantly improve your body’s ability to be efficient. A worst-case scenario for me would be an athlete that just runs on a treadmill the entire winter at a very narrow bandwidth of running paces.

“A good way of explaining this is that people talk about the way the Kenyans train. They do this famous long run in Iten where it’s a progressively descending pace. But what’s special about that workout is that they’re running on trails, gravel fire roads, wooded areas, and gradient changes. Probably the most powerful thing about that run is that they’re working on different surfaces, different terrains, different obstacles, different gradients, while they’re still working on a physiological stimulus.”

“That’s probably when people ask me what’s the number-one most important session for Ironman training: I would say go run on trails before anything else, because it builds resilience and strength, which is what you need for an Ironman.”

#8780. 10-Minute Morning Yoga Routine to Wake Up Your Entire Body

This quick yoga flow at home is, as the name promises, a continuously moving, flowy vinyasa practice for full-body flexibility that moves your body in all the ways you need. Rather than holding poses for an extended period of time, you’re moving with your breath in a fluid and rhythmic 10-minute yoga routine that will definitely energize you and target your back, hips, and hamstrings.

So if you woke up feeling a little sore or stiff, taking yourself through these movements can bring relief and get you feeling more comfortable in your body. I encourage you to choose a one-word intention for your day that you pause and focus on at the outset and throughout your practice. What is one word that captures how you want to feel today, what you want to focus on, or what matters to you right now?

No props are required although you are always welcome to use them anytime you would like more support.

You’re going to start by targeting the spine. From your hands and knees, your palms go underneath your shoulders, knees underneath your hips. As you inhale, lower your belly, lift your gaze and arch your back in Cow Pose.

As you exhale, reverse that motion. Thinking of pushing into your fingertips and knuckles, pushing the mat away from you, and letting your head release and your neck relax in Cat Pose.

And then go in between these two poses, getting into all parts of the spine, including the neck, upper back, mid back, lower back, all the way to your tailbone, trying to get that full range of motion.

Come back to hands and knees with a neutral spine.

Still on your hands and knees, lift your right leg and trace some circles with it, as big as you can, and then let’s reverse the direction of those circles. You’re simply trying to create movement through your right hip. You don’t need to overthink this one.

Step your right foot straight out to the side and press the outer edge of your foot against the floor. Lift yourself upright and reach your left arm overhead and toward the right in a side body stretch known as Gate Pose.

Come back to your hands and knees, tuck your toes, and hover your knees a little above the mat. You can probably feel your core engage.

Walk your feet back to keep your shoulders over your wrists in Plank Pose. Strongly press the mat away from you, drawing your lower belly inward and broadening through your upper back. Think of lengthening your tailbone toward your heels and drawing your lower belly inward and upward.

Let’s find Downward-Facing Dog. Lift your hips up and back, and peddle out your feet by straightening one leg and bending the other to stretch your ankles and calves. Keep your arms straight without locking your elbows. Feel the length through your spine.

Lower your knees to the mat and repeat the poses on your left side, including Hip Circles, Gate Pose, Hovering Tabletop, Plank, and Downward-Facing Dog.

From Downward-Facing Dog, reach your right leg toward the sky, bend your right knee, open your hip, and take one more of those big hip circles from your Three-Legged Dog.

From Down Dog, inhale as you step your right foot forward, spin your back foot almost parallel to the short side of the mat as if you were coming into Warrior 2. Exhale as you flow into Extended Side Angle, bringing your right forearm onto your right thigh and reaching your left arm overhead.

As you inhale, straighten your front leg and reach your right arm all the way back in Reverse Triangle.

Then exhale back into Extended Side Angle, sinking your hips a little lower. Repeat that flow twice more like this.

Bring both palms to the mat on either side of your right foot and find Pigeon Pose from here. So take your right knee behind your right wrist and reach your left leg straight back. Inhale as you come high onto your fingertips to lift and lengthen, then exhale as you bend forward.

Move in between the two shapes twice more as you undulate through the spine. Then the next time you lower yourself close to the mat, stay here for 5 long, slow breaths. Try to release tension through your shoulder blades and arms.

When you’re ready, lift yourself off the mat and find your Downward-Facing Dog. If you like, you can first come forward into Plank and then lower yourself to the mat and take Cobra. Then repeat these poses on your left side, starting with Three-Legged Dog, Dynamic Extended Side Angle, and Dynamic Pigeon.

Come back to Downward-Facing Dog. Pause here for several breaths.

Bring your knees to the mat and take a seat. As with most morning practices, I don’t include a Savasana in case you might be tempted to fall back asleep, but you’re always welcome to take it on your own.

Sit tall and roll your shoulders down and away from your ears. Maybe you bring your hands together at the front of your heart. Pause here for as long as you can.

Thank you so much for doing this quick vinyasa flow at home with me. May you feel really good and have gotten a boost of energy. Let me know what your intention is for the day ahead in a comment below.

#8779. Is Your Body Fat Percentage Holding Back Your Cycling Goals? The Answer Depends on Your Age and Ambition.

Your body fat percentage is a tool, not a judgment. Here’s are the recommended ranges that cyclists can use to support their goals.

For cyclists, body composition is a critical performance factor that goes beyond aesthetics. It directly influences climbing speed, power endurance, and recovery capabilities. Average body-fat percentage averages and recommendations shift as we age depending on individual goals, and whether we’re a recreational rider or a competitive cyclist pursuing maximum power-to-weight ratio.

Understanding age and typical body fat percentage ranges gives us valuable context for setting realistic and healthy body composition goals and determining whether our focus should be on fat loss, strength building, or overall health. (It’s important to note that body fat percentage and BMI (body mass index) are not the same thing.)

🚴🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you? Our Cycling for Weight Loss program will help you find confidence and consistency in your training.

There isn’t a universally “right” body-fat percentage. Ideal targets depend on sex, age, activity level, and specific goals, in addition to whether you’re prioritizing general health, recreational fitness, or competitive performance. However, there are commonly used target ranges per decade that coaches, trainers, and sports scientists use as healthy guidelines (which should be treated as approximate).

Let’s examine “average” body fat percentages guidelines by decade, what the average body fat percentages are for men and women in the United States, and the impact of different measurement methods (DEXA scan, home body fat scale, InBody scan) on results. These averages should be regarded as benchmarks for setting achievable, performance-oriented goals, not as rigid targets. They serve as a navigational tool rather than a mandatory destination.

20s: Competitive athletes: 6–10 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 11–15 percent, Healthy range: 12–20 percent

30s: Competitive athletes: 7–11 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 12–16 percent, Healthy range: 14–22 percent

40s: Competitive athletes: 8–12 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 13–17 percent, Healthy range: 16–24 percent

50s: Competitive athletes: 9–13 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 14–18 percent, Healthy range: 18–26 percent

60+: Competitive athletes: 10–14 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 15–19 percent, Healthy range: 20–28 percent

20s: Competitive athletes: 14–18 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 19–23 percent, Healthy range: 20–30 percent

30s: Competitive athletes: 15–19 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 20–24 percent, Healthy range: 22–32 percent

40s: Competitive athletes: 16–20 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 21–25 percent, 50s: Competitive athletes: 17–21 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 22–26 percent, Healthy range: 26–36 percent

60+: Competitive athletes: 18–22 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 23–27 percent, Healthy range: 28–38 percent

Cyclists specializing in climbing typically aim for the lower end of these ranges, though excessively rapid fat loss can compromise strength and power.

While the ranges above are recommended guidelines, the actual averages for folks according to the CDC look pretty different. The following data on average body fat percentage of men and women in the U. S. has been collected through the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.

It’s important to note that the body fat percentage measurement method really matters. Home scales that measure body fat percentage can be quite inaccurate according to researchers. In my own experience, an InBody scan (which is the measurement method I recommend for a more reliable assessment, by the way) revealed that my body fat percentage is several percentage points higher than what the home body fat scale I have been testing had measured.

However, even InBody results can fluctuate with hydration levels. DEXA scans offer the most stable results but are generally more expensive. The key is to track trends over time rather than focusing on single numbers.

When it comes to fat loss, aim for a safe and healthy pace of 0.5-1 percent of body weight per week, while prioritizing preserving lean mass through optimal protein intake and strength training. However, it can be tricky to determine how much of the body weight lost is fat, and factors like how lean someone already is, a person’s metabolism, and training intensity also play a role.

As an example, in one study of female volunteers on reduced-calorie diets, participants were assigned exercise programs of varying intensity. According to the researchers, the women doing a moderate exercise program lost 6.2 percent body fat over three months on average, which added up to being about 2 percent a month. The intense exercise group lost an average of approximately 10 percent body fat over the same time period, which comes out to around 3.3 percent per month.

Understanding body composition is a valuable tool for cyclists looking to optimize their performance and achieve their goals. By considering your age, sex, activity level, and using reliable measurement methods, you can set realistic targets and tailor your training and nutrition strategies accordingly. Remember, it's all about finding the right balance for your body and your goals.

Natascha is an editor and writer covering health, fitness, and the ways people move through the world. She’s been a NASM-certified personal trainer for more than a decade, with a background in functional strength training, corrective exercise, nutrition, and behavior change. She has additional CES, CNC, BCS, and SFC certifications. She is also a level-2 certified Spinning instructor. Her work has appeared in Bicycling, Runner’s World, and other outlets, and her experience spans both editorial and hands-on work across the fitness industry. Whether she’s writing about training, health, or performance, she’s most interested in making complicated topics useful, approachable, and helpful.

Earn Alaska miles through the Alaska Airlines Visa, Marriott Bonvoy transfers (3:1 ratio with 5K bonus per 60K), or direct purchase during sales. Target 60,000 miles for a one-way business class ticket.

Use JAL's own award search tool to check business class availability before contacting Alaska. Search 331 days out from your desired travel date. Look for flights showing "Partner Award" availability on JAL's calendar.

Verify your target flight operates a Boeing 787 or 777 with JAL's "Sky Suite" business class product. Older aircraft on some routes may have a less desirable cabin configuration. Check SeatGuru or JAL's fleet page.

Phone Alaska's award desk at 1-800-252-7522. Have your dates, route, and JAL flight number ready. The agent will search their system and process the redemption. Expect $25-$50 in taxes and fees.

Log into JAL.com with your confirmation number to select your specific seat and pre-order your meal. JAL offers both Western and Japanese cuisine options in business class, and the Japanese multi-course kaiseki meal is the experience worth choosing.

A sweet spot that punches far above its weight in cents-per-mile value

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you see it, and understanding it will help you recognize similar opportunities across the loyalty landscape.

Most major airline programs have shifted to dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate with demand, just like cash prices. Alaska Mileage Plan has largely resisted this for its partner awards. JAL Business Class from North America is priced at a flat 60,000 Alaska miles one way, period. It doesn't matter if it's Golden Week in Japan or a random Tuesday in February. The chart price holds.

This creates an extraordinary opportunity because JAL cash fares are not fixed. They respond to demand, fuel costs, seasonality, and competitive dynamics. When those fares rise — as they have substantially in recent years — your 60,000 miles buy proportionally more value. The inefficiency widens the more expensive the cash fare becomes.

Here's a detail that separates Alaska from many other programs: Alaska Mileage Plan charges zero fuel surcharges on any partner award booking. This is significant. Some programs (looking at you, British Airways Avios) pass through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $400–$800 to a theoretically cheap award. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket is taxes only — typically $50–$150 on a transpacific itinerary. Your 60,000-mile redemption costs you 60,000 miles plus roughly $100. Full stop.

The Transfer Path: Marriott Bonvoy Is Your On-Ramp

Alaska Mileage Plan has no direct credit card transfer partners in the traditional Chase/Amex/Citi sense. This is the most important nuance of this redemption to understand. You cannot transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards directly to Alaska. Instead, the primary transfer path runs through Marriott Bonvoy.

The ratio is 3 Marriott points to 1 Alaska mile, and transfers typically take 1 to 5 days to complete. There's also the well-known Marriott bonus: transfer 60,000 Marriott points and receive 5,000 bonus miles, meaning 60,000 Marriott points nets you 25,000 Alaska miles. This makes earning Alaska miles via Marriott cards (like the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless or Brilliant) a viable — if not the most efficient — path.

The more efficient earning strategy for most ChooseFI members is to apply directly for the Alaska Airlines Visa card, which regularly offers strong welcome bonuses, or to fly Alaska-operated flights. Miles in Alaska Mileage Plan never expire, which means you can accumulate patiently without pressure.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit almost no other major US program offers anymore. On a one-way award from the US to Japan, you could stop in Tokyo for several days, then continue to another destination, all for the same 60,000 miles. This is an advanced move that can double the value of a single award ticket.

Book at up to 331 days in advance — Alaska's booking window. For popular travel dates to Japan, searching early is strongly advised.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm the seats exist. Go to jal.com and use JAL's own award search tool. JAL releases excellent Business Class award inventory to partners — this is one of the best-availability premium cabin routes in the game — but you still want to verify before committing.

Search your target dates in "Award Booking" mode. Look for "J" class availability (Business Class). JAL's 787-9 Sky Suite III product operates on the Seattle–Tokyo Narita route, so filter for that routing specifically. Try flexible dates — a day or two of flexibility can reveal significantly more availability. You can search up to 330+ days out, so don't wait until the last minute.

You need 60,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per one-way Business Class ticket. Check your existing Alaska Mileage Plan balance at alaskaair.com. If you're short, your transfer path is Marriott Bonvoy at a 3:1 ratio — so 60,000 Alaska miles requires 180,000 Marriott Bonvoy points (though you'll receive a 5,000-mile bonus when transferring 60,000 Marriott points at a time, so plan accordingly).

Initiate transfers at marriott.com under "Transfer Points." Build in 1 to 5 days for the transfer to post to your Alaska account. Do not call Alaska to book until the miles are confirmed in your balance.

Alaska partner awards with JAL must be booked by phone — you cannot book JAL awards on Alaska's website. Call Alaska Mileage Plan at 1-800-252-7522. Have the following ready:

Tell the agent you'd like to book a partner award on JAL using miles. Give them the exact flight number and date. Agents are generally familiar with this redemption — it's a popular one.

Before you finalize, confirm the total cost. Alaska charges no fuel surcharges on partner awards, so your out-of-pocket should be taxes only. If an agent quotes you a surcharge, politely clarify — this is a known Alaska policy. The total cash component should be well under $200.

If your ideal dates show no availability, try these tactics: search plus or minus three days, look at alternate departure cities (JAL also operates from Los Angeles, Chicago, and New York), or set a calendar reminder to check again — JAL sometimes releases additional inventory closer to departure as business travelers book and cancel. The 331-day booking window means early searchers have the best selection.

Alaska Airlines is not part of any major airline alliance (Star Alliance, Oneworld, or SkyTeam), which gives it unusual freedom to set its own partner award pricing. While alliance members must coordinate pricing frameworks, Alaska negotiates individual deals with each partner airline. This independence is why Alaska can price JAL business class at 60,000 miles when alliance-member programs charge 70,000-100,000 miles for the same seats. The tradeoff is that Alaska's partner award availability can be more limited than what you would find through an alliance booking, making timing and flexibility critical.

Let's make this concrete. You and your partner are planning a trip to Japan in the spring — cherry blossom season, the dream itinerary for so many in the ChooseFI community.

The Route: Seattle (SEA) → Tokyo Narita (NRT) on JAL Flight 009, operated by a Boeing 787-9.

The Cash Price: Pull up JAL.com during late March and you'll routinely see Business Class fares at $7,000–$8,500 per person one way. For a couple, that's $14,000–$17,000 in cash for two seats in the premium cabin. Most people stare at that number and close the browser.

The Points Price: 60,000 Alaska miles per person. For two passengers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles plus approximately $200–$250 in taxes. Total cash outlay: roughly $225 for the pair.

The CPP: At a conservative $7,000 cash fare, 60,000 miles delivers 11.7 cents per point — nearly six times the standard benchmark for a great redemption.

JAL's inflight service is consistently ranked among the best in the world. The meal service features both Western and Japanese options, sake and premium spirits, and attentive crew who seem genuinely delighted to serve you. The 9–10 hour flight to Narita passes in quiet, restful comfort. You arrive refreshed.

For a couple targeting FI, spending 120,000 Alaska miles — earned largely through welcome bonuses and everyday spending — instead of $15,000+ in cash is the entire philosophy in action.

Alaska's booking window opens 331 days before departure. For cherry blossom season (late March through early April) and Golden Week (late April through early May), JAL Business Class award space is competitive. Set a calendar reminder and search on JAL.com starting at day 335 — then call Alaska the moment the window opens if you see available seats.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — one of the most underused benefits in the program. On a US-to-Japan routing, you could stop in Tokyo for four or five days, then continue to Osaka or another Japanese city (on a separate ticket), effectively getting a multi-city Japan trip from a single 60,000-mile award. Discuss this with the Alaska agent when booking.

Given Alaska's limited transfer partners, the most reliable path to a large Alaska miles balance is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card, which regularly offers welcome bonuses of 40,000–75,000 miles. Stack two cardholders in your household — you and your partner each earn a welcome bonus — and you have a round-trip business class redemption funded almost entirely from sign-up offers.

Marriott-to-Alaska transfers take 1 to 5 days and are irreversible. Never initiate the transfer until you've confirmed the award space exists on JAL.com. Transferring speculatively and then discovering the seat is gone is a painful and costly mistake.

While JAL does release excellent inventory — hence the availability score of 4 out of 5 — "year round" availability doesn't mean unlimited. Japanese holidays (Golden Week, Obon in August, New Year's) see compressed availability. The best open inventory is typically September through November and January through mid-February.

Alaska's policy is no fuel surcharges on partner awards, but always verify the final tax-and-fee total before giving your credit card number. Your total out-of-pocket should be well under $200 per ticket. If it's higher, ask the agent to itemize.

This redemption is built for the ChooseFI couple or solo traveler who has been intentionally accumulating Alaska miles — or Marriott Bonvoy points — and wants to experience transpacific Business Class without the $8,000 price tag. If Japan is on your bucket list and you're willing to do a phone call to complete the booking, this is one of the highest-value redemptions in the entire loyalty ecosystem.

Minimum points needed: 60,000 Alaska miles per person. A couple needs 120,000 miles for two one-way Business Class tickets.

This redemption is rated **moderate** — and that rating is honest. It's not beginner-friendly (rated 2 out of 5 for beginners), but it's absolutely achievable for anyone willing to learn the two-step process. **What makes it moderate:** First, earning Alaska miles is less straightforward than earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex points. Alaska has **no direct credit card transfer partners** in the major bank ecosystems, which means you can't funnel everyday Amex or Chase spend into Alaska miles directly. You're relying on Alaska co-branded credit cards or the Marriott Bonvoy transfer path. Second, partner award bookings **cannot be completed online** — you must call Alaska Mileage Plan. For travelers accustomed to booking everything digitally, this feels like friction. In practice, the call takes 15–20 minutes with a prepared agent and is genuinely straightforward. Third, while availability is rated 4 out of 5 (excellent by transpacific standards), you still need to plan ahead, particularly for peak Japan travel seasons. **Three tips to make it easier:** 1. **Start with the Alaska Airlines Visa card** — it's the most direct route to a large Alaska miles balance and regularly offers competitive welcome bonuses. 2. **Do your availability research on JAL.com before calling** — walk into that phone call with the flight number, date, and cabin class already confirmed. The booking becomes a five-minute transaction. 3. **Book 6–10 months out** for peak dates — this eliminates most of the availability stress and gives you time to transfer points if needed. If you've already booked one partner award by phone with any airline, this will feel familiar. If this is your first, the effort is absolutely worth it for a redemption worth 8–17 cents per point.

The best availability appears right at the 331-day booking window. Shoulder seasons like January-February and September-November tend to have more open seats. Cherry blossom season (late March through early April) and summer are the most competitive periods.

Marriott Bonvoy points transfer to Alaska at a 3:1 ratio. For every 60,000 Bonvoy points transferred, you receive 20,000 Alaska miles plus a 5,000-mile bonus, totaling 25,000 Alaska miles. To reach 60,000 Alaska miles, you would need approximately 135,000 Bonvoy points (factoring in the bonus on each 60K tranche).

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Alaska Mileage Plan to JAL business class is one of the best-kept sweet spots in travel rewards. At 60,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges, you get access to a world-class cabin at roughly half the mileage cost of competing programs. The earning path is narrower than programs with multiple transfer partners, but for anyone willing to build Alaska miles intentionally, the 8-13 cents per mile value on JAL business class to Japan is extraordinarily difficult to beat.
