#8714. Bicycling’s Gear of the Year 2027

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Great cycling gear doesn’t have to cost a fortune. These are the products our editors loved most this year.

There’s no shortage of new cycling gear promising to make your bike lighter, faster, or more comfortable. Over the past year, our editors have put those promises to the test on road and gravel rides, mountain bike trails, commutes, and in the workshop. For Gear of the Year, we’ve chosen the products that stood out most: the ones that solved a problem, made a ride more enjoyable, or delivered tangible performance that impressed us enough to recommend to you.

Our editors bring different perspectives to testing. Matt Phillips has tested bikes and gear for 30 years and has ridden more bikes than any other cycling journalist on the planet. Tara Seplavy has led product development at global bike brands, while Dan Chabanov has won national and elite titles in cyclocross and crit racing. Nearly all of us have worked in or managed bike shops.

Our picks reflect that range of experience and the different ways we ride. This year, we’ve organized them by price to make it easier to find something that fits your budget, whether you’re looking for a small upgrade or considering a bigger purchase. Whatever you choose, if it’s on this list, we think it will improve your ride.

Under $100 $100 to $300 $300 to $1,000 $1,000+

I get the skepticism about a product that seems to have figured out a problem that’s existed forever, but trust me, the Tyre Glider has made me completely rethink how I install tires. Instead of fighting the final few inches with my thumbs, you simply hook it under the bead and glide it around the rim. Until you use it, it just doesn’t make sense how simple and easy it is.

That mechanical advantage is especially useful with tight road tires and tubeless setups, where a conventional tire lever can feel precarious with carbon rims and spokes. It won’t replace a traditional lever for every job, but for the problem it’s designed to solve, it does it really well.

Last summer ended with me sporting a very prominent helmet vent hole tan line on my forehead. The reason was obvious: I avoided applying sunscreen there because every formula would sweat into my eyes. This summer I set out to find one that worked.

When I found Pelotan, I was skeptical of something marketed specifically to cyclists, but it works incredibly well. Although expensive, I found the 6-ounce bottle lasted me the entire season. It goes on light, evaporates quickly, smells nice, and most importantly doesn’t sting my eyes so I actually end up wearing it.

I often ride without gloves, so I’m picky about grips. After testing both the regular and fat versions of Ergon’s GDH Team, they’ve become my favorites for any bike built to get rowdy. The rubber is pleasantly soft and tacky, providing a secure hold with bare or gloved hands. Subtle fins under the fingers help keep my hands in place without forcing me to squeeze the bars hard.

Knipex makes some of the most enjoyable to use tools we have in the Bicycling workshop. The Pliers Wrench might look like an oddly shaped adjustable wrench, but its parallel jaws provide superior clamping force. It grips hardware securely without any slipping and marring.

These aren't bicycle-specific tools; they’re exceptionally good tools that happen to be incredibly useful around a bike. It comes in a range of sizes, but the 7 1/4-inch is the sweet spot: compact enough to live in a bike toolbox while still opening wide enough to handle most of the jobs I throw at it.

A front light is an easy addition to your road or gravel bike, but finding one that fits neatly on your cockpit can be tricky. Lezyne’s Road Drive 500 solves that problem with a slim, 75-gram body that tucks discreetly under a computer mount.

Despite its small size, the light offers a 500-lumen daytime flash and a 400-lumen mode for seeing the road or bike path after sunset. The replaceable battery lasts up to 55 hours in daytime flash mode or 4.5 hours in the 150-lumen enduro mode. Some computer mounts don’t let you adjust the beam's direction, but Lezyne includes a GoPro-style mount that lets you aim the light where you need it, at the expense of making the overall form factor a little less stealthy.

As a photographer and cyclist, I’m always looking for easier ways to carry cameras while riding. Peak Design’s Mobile Crossbody Multi Strap has become a useful way to keep small cameras and accessories secure and within reach.

Its mini quick-release mechanism lets me attach anchors to multiple devices and swap between them quickly. I’ve used it to carry a small gimbal camera while shooting the Philly Bike Race and as an added layer of security for cameras tucked into my pockets on rides. It’s also handy when traveling, letting me keep my phone or headphones tethered while making my way through an airport.

Spur Cycle’s R-Pro mirror gives road and gravel riders a simple way to see what’s happening behind them. Its alloy body and glass mirror have a high-end feel that looks at home even on a pricey carbon race bike, and it installs in just a few minutes.

I find it especially useful in heavy traffic, when a radar can be constantly pinging with notifications. A quick glance at the mirror helps me judge the distance to the vehicles behind me. It’s also handy on group rides to check that the person following me is still on my wheel. While the mirror doesn’t replace a radar, it never needs charging or pairing to a head unit.

I have found these Campagnolo 03 rotors to be categorically better than both SRAM and Shimano rotors while also being cheaper (a rare feat for a Campagnolo product).

The main issue I have with both SRAM and Shimano’s high-end road rotors is that after hard braking, they absorb enough heat to deform and briefly make noise. Riding the same roads after switching to Campagnolo rotors? No noise after hard braking. To me, this indicates the Campagnolo rotors manage braking heat better, which gives me more confidence in their performance; plus, silence is golden. At this point, I have replaced both Shimano and SRAM rotors with these Campagnolo ones and can recommend them highly as a better rotor alternative for any road bike groupset.

Back in 2025, I bumped into an old friend at Sea Otter. He was walking around with what might be the most curious saddle prototype I’ve ever seen. It looked like it was made from plastic and Styrofoam. It was also crazy light and, according to him, fully rideable.

Now, I finally have the production version. It’s still crazy light (146g on my scale). And those funky rails? An absolute joy to use. It’s such a simple solution: the saddle slides into the clamp instead of needing to partially take everything apart in some cases. But more importantly, as someone who has always tended to sit more forward, I love the wider nose on this saddle.

So far I’ve enjoyed about 500 miles on this saddle, and have been very, very pleasantly surprised. It has replaced the S-Works Power Evo saddle (which is quite popular and I also found very comfortable) on my road bike, but given how the Sixpack saddle is roughly a 1/3rd of the price, just as comfortable and 25 percent lighter, I feel no need to go back to the more expensive Specialized saddle.

Launched in 2025 as OEM equipment on Cervélo’s Áspero-5 gravel racer, Vittoria’s 700x42c version of its cotton-casing, all-season road tire is now available to the masses, and it’s excellent. The wider Corsa Pro Control features the cushion and grip of wider gravel rubber but rolls quickly, like a high-performance road tire. It’s the perfect upgrade for road riding on your gravel bike or building a go-fast all-road bike (provided you have enough clearance).

I’ve put roughly 1,000 miles on a pair of GP5000 TT TRs (set up tubeless) without a flat. That’s not something I can say about many high-performance tires, especially ones intended only for race days. I was actually a longtime Continental skeptic, but the GP5000 S TR started to change my mind, and the TT TR convinced me to finally change my tune. It combines competitive weight and low rolling resistance with a surprisingly long lifespan. If you want a fast race tire that can also handle training miles, the TT TR is worth a look.

In nearly 20 years of riding and racing, I avoided the urge to get custom insoles, even though I knew early on that my feet had some weird fit issues. This year, I finally gave in to my intrusive thoughts, and oh my god, I am not going back.

I truly didn’t think a custom insole would make as much of a difference as it did. But I’ve noticed all kinds of improvements, like my feet feeling much more stable and secure in the shoe without needing to ratchet down the closures. For the sake of experimentation, I even did a short ride with my previous comfortable (non-custom) insole setup, and I was shocked by how much discomfort I had gotten used to over the previous 20 years of riding. At this point, I would happily put custom insoles into a cheaper pair of shoes than ride stock insoles in a top-of-the-line shoe. I genuinely think the insole makes the bigger difference, and more riders should consider a pair for themselves.

At $190, Pearl Izumi’s Pi PRO/Black Mesh Jersey isn’t cheap, but it delivers the quality and performance I expect at that price. It’s a high-end racing jersey with understated looks, a combination that's hard to find in premium cycling kit.

The fit is cut for an aggressive position on the bike while maintaining excellent comfort and heat regulation. The paneled collar reduces pressure across the back of the neck, a common issue I’ve found with other aero-fit race jerseys. If you’re willing to pay a premium for a well-designed jersey but don’t want to look like a billboard, the Pi PRO/Black Mesh is a great option.

I am very stingy with my saddle recommendations because comfort is so uniquely personal to the rider. I know this because I ride a lot of different saddles, and I’ve discovered that only a very small minority are actually comfortable. But every so often I happen across a saddle that makes me say, “Oh, this one is special.” That’s the Ergon’s SRS Pro Carbon.

It’s plush without being squishy or saggy, offers even pressure distribution without feeling bulky, and is supportive without hot spots or pinch points. It’s also a rather good deal for a light (about 185 grams in an S/M size).

Typically, a European-made, carbon-railed saddle costs $300 or more, and that’s before you get into 3D-printed tops, so $220 seems almost reasonable.

I use a torque wrench almost every time I work on my bikes. Tightening parts to the correct torque helps prevent component failures, especially with carbon components, lightweight parts, or suspension linkages. Of the several torque wrenches in Bicycling’s workshop, I most often reach for Topeak’s Torq Stick Pro Digital.

The wrench adjusts from 1 to 20 Nm in one-tenth Nm increments. It beeps as you approach your selected torque and buzzes when you reach it. While it costs more than an analog wrench, I find it to be more precise and much easier to use, especially on parts that have torque ratings that include decimal points. Topeak’s set also includes common metric hex and Torx bits, an extender, an 8mm crowfoot for brake bleeds, and a small ratchet driver.

Heat training is a tool many of the world’s best bike racers use to prepare for hot summer races. The Core 2 Heat Sensor makes it easier to track and monitor that process, but I’ve found it useful even without fully optimizing my heat training.

The sensor monitors skin and core temperature and combines that information with heart-rate data to give you a heat-strain index. That makes it easier to gauge how your body is responding to the heat while riding. I use the sensor all summer to watch for spikes in my body temperature and take preventive measures before I overheat. With more summer events likely happening during periods of high heat, monitoring your body temperature more closely can be not just helpful, but tangibly beneficial.

The Q36.5 Dottore Pro jersey works across a wider range of temperatures than any other long-sleeve jersey I’ve tried. It holds enough heat to keep me comfortable on cool rides, but it also pulls moisture away from my body and feels cool enough for warmer days.

I’ve used it as a layer on a soaking-wet 50-degree ride, worn it on a 75-degree summer day, and ridden in it in plenty of conditions in between. On some of those rides, there were other pieces of clothing I would have changed, but I would have picked the same jersey every time. Its versatility means it can replace multiple layers, making it well worth the asking price.

The Varia RearVue 820 is Garmin’s first full update to its successful radar light in nearly six years. It delivers more information to compatible Garmin Edge head units, offers brighter light, supports USB-C charging, provides longer battery life, and extends detection range. On the road, the RearVue 820 feels like a noticeable step up from other radar units—notably, it consistently detects vehicles approaching from behind earlier than other devices.

Same-speed tracking was another revelation. Not having to constantly check whether the car that dropped off my screen was still following me or had turned into a driveway is something no other radar unit does reliably, and it's a big reason I would choose the 820 over other units. If you’re using a modern Garmin cycling computer that supports advanced tracking features, the Garmin Varia RearVue 820 is more than just an update to the RTL 515. It’s a big step forward in cycling radar technology.

But even if you’re not using the latest Edge device, my comparative testing showed the 820 was always the first radar to detect an approaching car, sometimes by several seconds. Sure, things like better battery life, a more convenient charging standard, and a brighter light are great. But when it comes to cycling radars, better, faster detection is king, and right now the RearVue 820 wears that crown.

The Apex Aeon bibs are stupid expensive, but great bibs are one of the few pieces of cycling equipment worth splurging on. These have become my favorite pair for long, hard, hot rides, maintaining their support and comfort from start to finish.

The straps and lowers are thick and feel almost overbuilt, a welcome change from cycling apparel that can feel wispy and fragile. The chamois is medium-thick and the firmest I can remember using, but it’s fantastically comfortable without feeling like a diaper. Like the rest of the bib, it shines brightest on longer rides. I’ve worn almost nothing else this summer, and whenever I ride in a different pair, I invariably wish I’d grabbed these instead.

It is no understatement to say SRAM is on a roll. Thanks to a combination of performance, features, and impeccable timing, its drivetrains are the benchmarks for mountain, gravel, and road riding at the moment. On the road, the newest Red (E1) stormed into the market with superbly comfortable hoods, brilliant brakes, and excellent shifting. One would be wise never to count Shimano out, but Red E1 announced to the world that it had forever altered the drivetrain status quo.

Other Bicycling editors and I have long argued that top-of-the-line drivetrains, especially in the electronic era, are never the smart buy. Give up a bit of weight, and you can get all the performance of a brand’s top-tier group for a lot less money. And that’s the case with SRAM’s Rival E1. It offers all the performance and improvements of Red E1, along with SRAM’s impressive ecosystem interoperability. The bonus buttons on the hoods are the only feature you might miss: Red and Force have them; Rival does not. Aside from those, Rival E1 offers the benchmark performance of Red E1 without the painful hit to the wallet.

In any given year, I ride between 20 and 30 different bikes (usually with a variety of wheels), and I will also likely test anywhere between five and ten standalone wheelsets. That is, I ride a lot of different road wheels every year, and these Rovals earned my Gear of the Year endorsement because I keep coming back to them.

One of the things I like most: I think Specialized has cracked the secret sauce with their carbon spokes. Every other carbon-spoked wheel I have tried has a much harsher ride than a traditional steel-spoke wheel. Both the Rapide Sprint and the Rapide CLX III feel more like traditional wheels, just with a bunch of weight lopped off. I keep coming back to the deeper Sprint version over the more all-around CLX III because I don’t really feel the roughly 90g difference, but I definitely notice the extra speed on flat and rolling terrain. It’s pretty wild that Specialized has managed to make a set of 60-ish mm deep wheels (63 mm and 58 mm deep, to be exact) this light while also making them feel so smooth.

#8712. The Best Black Friday Running Shoe Deals Are Here—Save on Brooks, Asics, Saucony, and More

These Black Friday deals include daily trainers, stability shoes, and marathon racers.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note: Prices and availability are subject to change. Check your size—and maybe a different color—to see if it’s in stock.

From Brooks to Asics to Saucony, these running shoes are on sale now at amazing discounts for Black Friday. Now’s the perfect time to score all kinds of trainers for early winter runs and races. Many of these shoes are on our best running shoes list and are discounted by up to 48 percent.

And when we say there are good deals, we mean it. Right now, Black Friday is giving us amazing running shoe sales. You’ll find favorite daily trainers and marathon racing shoes. Everything you need is here: If you’re a beginner looking for a shoe with Goldilocks cushioning—here’s your guide to point you in the right direction and help you save big.

These shoes are available in limited colors and sizes, so race there fast!

The GlideRide Max is a whopping 53 percent off. It’s pumped with FF Blast Max and FF Blast Plus midsole foams for a max-cushioned ride with smooth toe-off, thanks to Asics’s Guidesole tech.

“This is an awesome shoe—one of my favorites I’ve ever tested,” said Senior News Editor Theo Kahler, who trains at 6:30 pace. “It’s got a lot of plushy comfort without feeling clunky or slow. The ride is one of the best I’ve gotten from any daily trainer. It’s also a very soft shoe—not necessarily in the foam, but the insoles and collar are very soft and comfortable.”

The women’s Glideride Max 2 is also currently on sale for 24%.

Truly, the Endorphin Pro 4 is my personal favorite marathon shoe. The fit isn’t compressive like the Nike Vaporfly 4, and the ride isn’t as volatile as the Nike Alphafly 3 (or, for that matter, the Saucony Endorphin Elite 2).

Layers of Pwrrun PB and Pwrrun HG foam provide high rebound and support over hours of road racing. The Speedroll rocker profile encourages fast turnover.

“The Saucony Endorphin Pro 4 is a great upgrade in the Endorphin Pro lineup,” said tester Greg Jaindl. “I have worn all previous versions of the Endorphin Pro line, and this version is a great update without changing what works too much.

I think the best part of the shoe is its snappy, responsive ride! Saucony has nailed the smooth transition with its Speedroll technology. The Pro 4 also makes sure to put enough cushioning in the shoe that you’re protected for longer distances, but not making it too squishy that you lose out on the energy return.”

The Gel-Cumulus 28 is cushioned with FF Blast Max foam so it feels like running on clouds with every step. The PureGel tech in midsole enhances that softness, absorbing shock and encouraging you to continue forward.

“Compared to other daily trainers I have tested, the Asics Gel Cumulus 28 is a perfect, stable, trainer,” said tester Caroline Lennon. “They were exceptionally comfortable and I never had any pain, discomfort, or nagging injury crop up in my time with these shoes.”

The Peg 42 has a full-length Air unit to deliver a propulsive ride. The ReactX is also updated to be even more responsive. A nod to Nike’s origin story is that waffle tread outsole, which provides reliable traction.

“What I like most is that it feels smooth, with a great rolling ride, but also supportive underfoot,” said Peg 42 tester Molly Sunderlin. “It feels easy to run quickly in, but also like I can do a two-hour long run without getting sore underfoot.”

Just as popular as the Ghost, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is a top-rated trainer that we’ve included in our Best Running Shoes and Best Walking Shoes guides. It’s a go-to trainer for runners looking for a softly cushioned shoe that provides stability when you need it. The guide rails system is the brand’s holistic support tech; dense foam located on the medial and lateral sides of the shoe acts as bumpers to help with knee and ankle alignment.

“My favorite feature of the shoe is the ride,” said tester and overpronator Peter Vuong. “It’s very smooth, has the right amount of bounce, and transitions from heel to toe very nicely. It might be one of the best shoes I’ve ever worn in terms of the ride.”

Think of the Clifton 10 as your go-to everyday trainer. The shoe has an accommodating fit (wide-foot runners didn’t feel squeezed) and a bouncy ride. Whether you’re a new runner or following a run/walk marathon training plan, the ClifTEN is your cushioned companion, delivering a high-rebound ride in a max-cushioned package.

“The Hoka ClifTEN is probably one of the most comfortable shoes I have run in,” said Assistant Commerce Photo Editor Saba Ahmed. “From the roomy and cushioned midsole area to the cushioned arch support, these are a pair of shoes that you can truly go run in right out of the box. As a wide shoe wearer, I felt the wide sizing was accurate and felt no discomfort in the mid area and felt plenty of flexibility by the toes.”

The Tecton X 3 is a super shoe for trail runners and ultrarunners. It’s prepped for gnarly terrain with its grippy Vibram Megagrip outsole, protective gaiter-style collar, and resilient Matryx quick-dry upper.

The shoe has carbon-fiber winglets in its midsole to provide stability on uneven surfaces and propulsion.

“This is a GREAT shoe, it has many unique features that will help train and ultimately race,” said tester Mike Parmer. “Starting with the built-in sock to protect your ankle while running and the aggressive cushion. Compared to other Hoka trail shoes, these are by far the best and lightest shoe I have tested.”

At 46 mm, the Hyperion Max 3 is a towering super trainer with responsive PEBA DNA Gold foam in its midsole. We like it for marathon training or even racing (as long as you’re not an elite who must follow 40 mm or less stack-height guidelines).

“I love the Hyperion Max: This shoe is a great training shoe for getting those long miles in with tired feet. It takes the pounding out when running on roads; it really absorbs the impact well and also feels easy to push the faster miles as well,” said tester Ricky Snyder.

The Arahi 8 was included in our Gear of the Year buying guide. Hoka truly updated the cushioning and flexibility of the shoe, righting the wrongs of the previously stiff and firm seventh iteration.

New to the Arahi 8 was the H-Frame support system, an H-shaped midsole component that helps stabilize your ride. The brand also added 3 mm of foam in the heel. The result is softer landings, especially for heel strikers.

Wow! The Brooks Ghost 17 is now on sale! It’s the go-to daily trainer we recommend to vets and newbs alike. The Ghost 17 has even softer but supportive DNA Loft v3 foam cushioning in the heel and forefoot.

“I would rate the Brooks Ghost 17 as one of the best shoes I’ve run in on the road in a long time,” said tester Liz Fones. “When I first put them on, I felt like they might be a bit constrictive compared to the Hokas I’m used to wearing. However, once I started running, I felt like an old friend was by my side, giving me the boost I needed!”

The Fresh Foam X 1080 v14 is a favorite for its plush ride and accommodating fit. New Balance offers multiple widths, so you’ll be happy to know your wide or narrow foot will find a comfy medium in this cushy trainer.

“Overall, I thought the foam X 1080 was a solid shoe,” said tester Nick Miller. “I used it both for speed work and while training for a marathon. It performed well over short distances and on long runs. I tested the previous version last year and was surprised by some of the improvements, especially in performance. The one downside I noticed was that it is a little heavier than what I am used to running in. I also really enjoyed the shoe's rocker. As a pretty big heel striker, that helps with any heel pain I get from my mechanics.”

This super trainer just came out last fall, and it’s already on sale for $160. We like it for its propulsive ride and shock-absorbing cushioning.

I wore the Sonicblast on a 16-mile run during my Boston Marathon training block. Despite the 46mm stack height, the shoes didn’t feel unstable. They also made my mid-run race-pace tempos more bearable.

“The Sonicblast felt like a very good option for all types of training runs, and for this reason, I love it,” said Trevor Conde. “It’s versatile and useful on any day of training. I would genuinely use this for any type of run: easy miles, tempo, speed work, hard intervals, long runs, etc. I love putting it on for an easy run and letting the legs just feel more pop and quick turnover than I normally feel on an easy mileage day.”

We love the Guide 18 because it’s a stability shoe that’s just so darn comfy. Don’t believe me? Then read it straight from tester Dave Block’s shoe feedback form:

“The first time I tried on the shoe, I cracked a big smile. I *loved* the feel. It’s just so darn soft and comfortable inside! It put me in a positive frame of mind before I went out the door. If memory serves, this shoe has the most comfortable interior of all the ones I’ve wear-tested.

“The shoe features Saucony’s Center Path technology, which uses asymmetric midsole geometry and a wider midfoot. This translates to unobtrusive support for overpronators and late-onset overpronators alike.”

Another great choice for running and walking, the Gel-Nimbus is known for its soft, pillowy midsole, ideal for recovery days or long miles on the road. FF Blast Plus cushioning, paired with Asics’s PureGel, provides an incredibly cozy platform that molds to your foot.

“From the moment I put on the Asics Nimbus 27, it was clear that the Nimbus was an outstanding running shoe, offering an excellent balance of cushioning, comfort, and support,” said tester Dee Koutsourais. “Having run in a wide range of shoes within the neutral category and even those on the periphery, the Nimbus 27 is definitely a strong contender in the max-cushion lineup. The plush, cloud-like feel of the midsole, combined with great durability and breathability, makes it an ideal choice for long-distance runners and anyone on their feet for extended periods.”

The Ghost Max is a plusher version of your favorite daily trainer. The shoe is a terrific walker or mattress-soft shoe for the injury-prone. Its accommodating fit creates a roomy footbed for orthotics wearers, and the DNA Loft v3 foam delivers ultimate shock absorption for sore knees and long efforts.

“The Brooks Ghost Max 3 serves great as an everyday trainer for beginner to intermediate runners who prioritize comfort first and are looking to log many casual miles,” said tester James Prekopa. “The relatively light and lean ride makes it easy to enter a flow state. I found this shoe to be ideal for solid surfaces like pavement and concrete. These surfaces let you maximize the shoe's comfort features without feeling like you’re sinking too much. This shoe is for someone who prioritizes comfort first, stability second, and performance last.”

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

#8711. The Best Compact Rowing Machines for Small Spaces in 2025

A smaller footprint doesn’t mean you have to miss out. Here are the best compact rowing machines for a top-notch workout.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

If you’re limited on space, don’t let the length of a rowing machine deter you. While there are many great rowing machines on the market, there are also some awesome compact alternatives that offer all the same tech features you’ll find in other cardio machines.

During our search for the best compact rowing machine, we found an array of excellent standalone options and options that fit in well with other top-rated home gym equipment. We considered the overall footprint and other key features, and scoured the reviews to see what users had to say about each product. Below is our list of the best compact home rowing machines available.

The rowing machines included in this list were carefully selected based on what most users would want out of a rowing machine, keeping in mind that they needed to have a smaller footprint and folding or upright storage options. We evaluated each choice based on size, portability, cost, high-tech features, versatility, and durability. We also scoured the reviews to see what users had to say about each rowing machine.

On the Hydrow website, the Hydrow Wave is rated 4.6/5 stars with over 9,000 reviews at the time of writing. It’s the brand’s compact, budget-friendly option for those who want to elevate their at-home workout routine. The length is just 80 inches, which is the shortest on this list, and the overall size is 30 percent shorter than the original Hydrow Rower. You cannot fold it, but there is the option to store it upright using The Hydrow Wave Vertical Anchor. This is a wall-mounted strap that holds the rower upright. It costs an additional $190, which is a bit on the pricey side.

The frame is made of aluminum and steel. It has a flat anthracite polymer body, which is a durable and lightweight material. The handle has an ergonomic design for a low-stress grip, and the strap is made from water- and rot-resistant polyester webbing. It also has a patented electromagnetic drag system that mimics the experience of rowing on open water.

Overall, the reviews on the Hydrow website are positive, and many mention how quiet the machine is and how much they like the small footprint. One review says, “The machine is such great quality. It’s quiet and sleek looking.” The critical reviews make up 3 percent of the overall reviews and state issues like non-working parts being delivered. However, Hydrow has responded to each review to resolve any issues.

The NordicTrack RW700 has a 10-inch HD touchscreen you can tilt and pivot to follow along with an iFIT workout led by your favorite trainer on or off the rower. An iFIT subscription is $39 per month, and you’ll have access to live and on-demand classes. Membership to the fitness app is not required to use the rower; however, you won’t have access to trainer-led classes without it.

A trainer-led rowing workout gives you the option to row on the open water for a more scenic experience, and there are also studio sessions. The resistance is adjusted automatically among 26 resistance levels during each class, so you don’t need to worry about stopping to make changes. The oversized foot pedals have adjustable nylon foot straps with quick release, which is excellent for those who want to incorporate movements off the rower into their workout.

The rail is 87 inches long and made from durable steel. It has an inertia-enhanced flywheel, so it should maintain a smooth rotation. If you have a shared space, the NordicTrack RW700 rower has a magnetic resistance system that creates tension against the flywheel without touching, making it a quieter option. After your workout, this magnetic rowing machine can be moved using the front wheels, but it can’t be folded.

The flywheel has been designed to maintain inertia and rotate smoothly, and the steel rail is oversized to help keep you stable. The large, pivoting foot pedals with adjustable nylon straps keep your feet in place, and the seat is molded with comfort in mind.

If you like to incorporate other movements into your rowing workout or train off of the rower, the Echelon Row-s has a 22-inch HD touchscreen that can be flipped 180 degrees. While an Echelon Fit subscription is not required, the extra $35/month workout app gives you access to over 40 live classes and more than 1,000 on-demand workouts from its library, including rowing, biking, running, and functional training classes.

The ergonomic design of the seat and the ability to adjust the foot platforms to a comfortable position help you maintain proper posture and alignment. If you’re short on space, the length goes from 84 inches long to just 41 inches long when folded. On the Echelon website, this rower is rated 4.6/5 stars. “The machine looks great, operates very quietly, and gives a great workout no matter your level,” says reviewer Brett P.

Dimensions: 87.02" L x 22.0" W x 47.24" H

Storage: Folds in half for vertical storage

Available programming: Live and on-demand workouts, scenic rows

The NordicTrack RW600 balances great tech features and an accessible price, making it a great value. The 10-inch screen is an excellent option for those who want to take instructor-led classes using an iFIT membership. NordicTrack’s patented Silent Magnetic Resistance can be adjusted up to 26 levels automatically in an iFIT class or manually as needed.

The pivoting foot pedals are oversized, and the nylon straps keep your feet secure. The handlebar has a soft grip, and the molded seat is designed to help you feel comfortable. When your workout is finished, the NordicTrack RW600 can be folded and stored out of the way.

What factors should you consider before you pull the trigger on a rower? Here’s what we’d recommend you take into account as you ponder your purchase decision:

Once you’ve decided on your rower location, it’s a good idea to measure the length, width, and height of your space to determine what size machine works best. You’ll want to measure height to see if you have enough clearance for rowers to be stored upright.

After measuring, think about how much you’re willing to spend. Take into consideration any additional costs such as a monthly subscription. Some rowers also have add-ons for purchase, such as a lumbar support system or seat upgrade.

Ask yourself: How many levels of resistance do I need? Am I looking for an HD touchscreen with trainer-led classes or do I prefer a more simplistic display? Other features such as a magnetic resistance system may be important if you’re in a shared space and need a quieter machine. The rower’s maximum height and/or weight capacity may also play a role in your decision as well.

Rowing allows you to implement low-impact, cardio-based training, and you can adjust the resistance for a strength-focused session. It’s a full-body workout that uses 86 percent of your muscles. With each stroke, you’re using your core and legs for the initial pull and finishing the rowing movement by using your upper body. Since you’re in a seated position, there’s less pressure on your knee and ankle joints.

Getting all four types of exercise (endurance, strength, balance, and flexibility) has benefits, according to The National Institute of Health (NIH). A rowing machine can be utilized for two types: endurance and strength. Many rowing machines have built-in programs or subscriptions that offer classes geared toward building strength and endurance.

Rowing is a great way to build strength and endurance while working various muscle groups. There are choices to suit a variety of budgets with different storage options and sizes. Figuring out how much space you have, your price range and the features you’d like will help you choose the best compact rowing machine for you.

The machines on this list range from just over $700 to around $2,000. You can find a rower in your price range, but if you opt for a rower under, say, $200, you may be compromising quality.

Typically, rowing machine length ranges between six to nine feet with more compact options at six or seven feet long.

The level of resistance that’s best for you depends on your fitness level, experience, and goals. Overall, you don’t want your workout to be too easy or so challenging you don’t accomplish the goal of your training session.

Compact rowing machines usually have air or magnetic resistance, and some options implement both.

#8708. 6 Core-Strengthening Exercises to Spice Up Your Routine

Grab one dumbbell and challenge your core with these moves.

The core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics. But your torso muscles—which include your abs, back, glutes, and hip flexors—play a crucial role in cycling that goes way beyond looks.

Research shows just how important core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine. One 2019 study, published in PLoS One, found that an eight-week core training program improved balance and core endurance (which you need to maintain posture through long miles) in the 21 college athletes who participated. Another research review, published in Frontiers in Physiology in 2022, says core training should have a place in all athletes’ training programs.

The authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability. The authors also write that these core strength benefits help prevent “energy leaks,” therefore leading to better performance.

To help you gain these benefits of a strong midsection, you need a solid workout to add to your routine. Thankfully, Noam Tamir, C.S.C.S., founder and CEO of TS Fitness in New York City, created this dumbbell core-strengthening workout.

In addition to the research that proves the benefits of core strength for athletes, the moves Tamir chose for this workout make an ideal mix for those looking to improve performance. Not only will the moves improve your stability in an upright posture, allowing you to ride and breathe more efficiently, but they also target the core from multiple angles, hitting every muscle of the torso.

Even better: While these moves resemble familiar core exercises, each one has a creative spin. This means they not only challenge your body in fun new ways, but also engage your brain.

How to use this list: Do each exercise below, in order, for the reps listed. Repeat for 3-4 rounds. Rest as needed between exercises and rounds.

Tamir demonstrates the exercises in the video above so you can learn proper form. You will need one light to medium dumbbell for this workout. An exercise mat is optional.

Why it works: The half-kneeling halo exercise focuses on trunk stability. “It works the core at 360 degrees because the dumbbell is moving around the body while you’re maintaining an upright position,” Tamir says. You do the same thing on a ride—hold a strong posture and upright body position while your arms and legs move.

How to do it: Start kneeling, right knee on ground, and left foot planted in front, both knees bent 90 degrees. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chin. Keeping torso and lower body steady, circle dumbbell clockwise around head. Elbows stay close to head. Return to chin. Repeat in other direction. Do 8-10 reps in each direction. Switch leg stance each round.

Why it works: Target the obliques with this rotational move. You’ll also hit the rectus abdominis (those six-pack looking abs) and work on coordination of the upper and lower body, Tamir explains.

How to do it: Start seated on floor. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chest. Lean back slightly, and lift legs off floor, hips and knees bent about 45 degrees. Bring dumbbell to outside of left hip by rotating torso to right and extend left leg straight out, foot lowering close to floor. Keep shoulders down and back. Next, bend left knee and extend right leg out, lowering foot close to floor and lift dumbbell up and over to the right, rotating torso to the right. Bring weight back down to outside of left hip, as you extend right leg out and pull left knee back in. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Why it works: This explosive movement focuses on the hips. “The core is not limited to just the abdominal muscles,” Tamir says. “You also need the whole body to create power, strength, and endurance.” This exercise gets more muscles in on the action, while the hinge motion helps to improve riding, especially during acceleration, he adds.

How to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart, dumbbell in right hand down by side. Hinge at hips, by sending butt straight back, dumbbell reaching behind you. Keep back flat and core engaged. Using glutes, drive feet into floor and extend hips. Let the power of your glutes send dumbbell forward and up to shoulder height. Engage core, like you’re hitting a standing plank position at the top. Let the momentum of the dumbbell guide you back into a hinge position. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps.

Why it works: This anti-rotation exercise works the deep core muscles, including the transverse abdominis that wraps around your midsection, and the multifidus, the posterior core muscles that protect your spine, Tamir explains. “It also helps to stabilize the pelvis to reduce risk of injury,” he adds, and aids in strong posture by working the back.

How to do it: Start in a plank position, left hand on a dumbbell, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Feet should be slightly wider than hips. Pull left elbow straight up, dumbbell reaching to ribcage. Lower back down. Repeat. Keep hips as steady as possible. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Why it works: The pullover crunch focuses mainly on the rectus abdominus (the muscles on the front of the torso) which helps to stabilize the spine and, in turn, maintain good form, Tamir says.

How to do it: Lie faceup, holding a dumbbell vertically with both hands overhead, dumbbell behind you, arms extended. Bend knees, feet planted on floor. Pull dumbbell overhead and crunch up, lifting head, neck, and shoulders off floor. At the same time, lift feet off floor, driving knees toward arms. Slowly lower back down, dumbbell hovering off floor behind you, and feet hovering off floor in front of you. Repeat. Do 12-15 reps.

Why it works: This is a great move for stabilizing the spine, while teaching abdominal bracing, Tamir says. The weight on one side also forces the core to resist rotation, which you need for efficiency on the road.

How to do it: Lie face up. Hold dumbbell in right hand over shoulder, arm straight. Extend left arm overhead, biceps by ear. Lift head, neck, shoulders, and legs a few inches off floor. Use legs to rock back and floor, maintaining the hollow body position. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat with dumbbell in left hand.

#8707. A Runner Took a Midrace Puff of Weed at the NYC Marathon. Now, She’s Disqualified.

This Houston attorney lost her official result, but kept her medal—and her sense of humor.

Having your first marathon result erased after months of training might be enough to send anyone into a downward spiral. Andrea Sager, though, has been getting some serious mileage out of the bad news on Instagram.

"Damn, I can't send my 5:54 to Boston now 💀," the 35-year-old joked in a recent post, referencing the news that she’d been disqualified from the 2026 NYC Marathon despite crossing the finish line.

The Houston attorney and mother of two found out she was DQ’d days after the November 1 race when footage surfaced of her smoking marijuana on the course. The moment she decided to accept a puff from a spectator was caught on video, and New York Road Runners subsequently removed her finish time from its records.

As far as the rules go, there's little room for debate. NYRR's Code of Conduct explicitly prohibits "smoking, vaping, or use of electronic smoking devices, tobacco products, or marijuana products" in the starting corrals, on the course, and in the finish area, with the restriction extending 1,000 feet beyond those locations.

In a video explaining her disqualification, Sager acknowledged breaking the rules and said she understood the decision. Even so, she claimed she wasn’t the only runner to drink alcohol or smoke weed during the race, and suggested the difference was having the moment seen by millions of people on social media.

"I wasn't planning on smoking weed on the course, but I was in so much pain and needed something to help me finish," she told the New York Post.

Sager hasn't let the penalty spoil her memories of race day. Her original finish-line recap described a grueling 26.2 miles that involved "approximately 47 mental breakdowns," although she was thrilled to check the race off her bucket list. She later reminded followers that the experience could not be taken away from her.

She'd been having plenty of fun long before arriving in New York, too. One prerace Instagram video joked about giving up dating apps in favor of training for a marathon, while her bright pink marathon shirt doubled as a personal advertisement. The front read, "Andrea, 35, Single. Great Credit. Bad Judgment," while the back added, "Looking for a man with more endurance than my ex."

Her latest social media introduction has since acquired another word: "35. Single. Great credit. Poor judgment. Disqualified."

Sager still has her finisher medal, and the extra attention has brought some unexpected opportunities.

"I'm talking with the brands now, so there's a lot of upside, but still annoying," she told the Post.

Sager said she was told she can participate in future NYRR events, despite the removal of her November 1 result. Runner's World contacted the organization for comment and confirmation of her eligibility but received no response.

As for racing plans, Sager said she has HYROX Houston on her calendar for April 2027. And someone in her Instagram comments has suggested a shirt idea for her next event:

"I smoked weed at the NYC marathon and all I got was a DQ."

#8706. The Best Protein Powders for Weight Loss, According to a Certified Nutrition Coach

Protein powder can help you maintain muscle mass while eating in a calorie deficit. We tested more than 100 protein powders and found nine we think are best for weight loss.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Feb 19, 2025

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

When someone says they want to lose weight, what they really mean is they want to shed excess body fat. However, without a well-designed plan in place, a calorie deficit leads you to lose both fat and valuable muscle tissue. To minimize muscle loss, it’s crucial to incorporate resistance training, quality sleep, and a high-protein diet into your regular routine.

Protein plays a multifaceted role in weight management, influencing factors like hunger levels, metabolism, and muscle preservation. While heavy resistance training provides the necessary stimulus, signaling to the body that existing muscle should be retained, a high-protein diet ensures the body has an ample supply of amino acids. This prevents your body from metabolizing muscle tissue for energy.

The best protein powders provide a convenient and lean source of the muscle-building macronutrient, helping you hit your daily protein goals while also maintaining a calorie deficit. We tested more than 100 protein powders and selected nine products we think are best for weight loss.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

We chose these products based on a number of factors, including:

I chose Transparent Labs as the best protein powder for weight loss because it has a very high ratio of protein to the total number of calories: 28 grams to 130 calories. This helps you maximize protein consumption during a caloric deficit, which helps prevent you from losing muscle while you’re losing weight. It’s also third-party tested, Informed Choice certified, and completely artificial ingredient-free. And it comes in 15 flavor options.

I’ve tried a number of different flavors from Transparent Labs and Chocolate Peanut Butter is by far my favorite, followed closely by Mocha. I found they mixed easily in both a blender and a conventional shaker bottle. Whenever I’m trying to cut weight, I find this delicious protein powder helps curb my sweet tooth and tide me over between meals.

While I didn’t personally experience this, some customer reviews mention it can be challenging to get in contact with Transparent Labs’ customer service team.

Jacked Factory Authentic Iso has 25 grams of protein per serving, 2 grams of carbohydrates, and just 0.5 grams of fat, which is the least amount of fat of any powder on our list. If you’re looking to lose weight, this macronutrient profile will help keep you on the right track. However, something to keep in mind: This protein powder is sweetened with sucralose, which is an artificial sweetener—studies link these sweeteners to increased cancer risk. Additionally, unlike most brands on our list, Jacked Factory doesn’t do third-party testing on its products. This means there isn’t a guarantee the ingredients are pure and match the ingredient label.

Kessler tried Jacked Factory Authentic Iso and was impressed. “This is the only protein powder I’ve tried that didn’t settle at all,” he says. “I found it a bit too sweet, but if you’re looking for a powder that tastes like dessert, you should opt for this one.”

If you’re looking for one of the best vegan protein powders that also works with a weight loss diet, Ka’Chava is a great choice. This vegan protein powder is marketed as a “whole-body meal,” which means it’s designed as a meal replacement rather than an addition to a meal or snack, like the other protein powders on our list. That’s why the calorie, carbohydrate, and fat counts (240, 25 grams, and 7 grams, respectively), are higher. The carb count is high for those on a low-carb diet, so that’s something to look out for. However, it packs in 25 grams of plant protein, derived from a combination of peas, brown rice, and quinoa, which will help preserve muscle while on a weight loss diet.

Tester Zoe Ettinger, a C.N.C.-in-training, uses this protein powder often. “I’m a big fan of Ka’Chava. It tastes delicious mixed in a smoothie with some frozen blueberries,” she says. “I also like that it also has adaptogens, probiotics, greens, and probiotics. I notice a difference in how good I feel when I take Ka’Chava regularly,” she says.

One thing to note about Ka’Chava is that it is the most expensive option on our list at $79.99 for a 15-serving bag. While the price reflects the fact that this protein powder is intended as a meal replacement, it’s still a big investment.

I chose Nutricost as the best protein powder for weight loss available on Amazon because its calorie and macronutrient profile is ideal for shedding pounds. Nutricost has a high protein content per serving, which is important for weight loss as protein can help enhance satiety and preserve muscle mass while in a deficit. With minimal fat and carbohydrates, this protein ensures you get the maximum protein intake without the added calories, making it an ideal choice for those looking to lose weight efficiently.

The taste and mixability of this protein are also top-notch. I tested the Vanilla flavor; it blended excellently in both milk and water and had an authentic vanilla taste profile. Despite using artificial sweeteners, which often make products sickly sweet, I found the sweetness level to be on point. However, if you’re trying to avoid artificial sweeteners, choose Promix or Transparent Labs, which use natural sweeteners.

Huel is our favorite meal replacement for weight loss because it has a great protein-to-carb ratio. Huel has 40 grams of protein per serving, the most of any protein powder on our list, and 24 grams of carbs. While this might be more carbs than ideal for those on a keto diet, it’s a solid portion for most. Carbs are an essential nutrient and according to experts, you can consume 100 to 150 grams a day and still lose weight.

Kessler tried Huel in Chocolate and Vanilla. “The Chocolate flavor was great, probably because it uses real cocoa powder, which gave it an authentic chocolate flavor,” he says. “The Vanilla wasn’t as good—it didn’t really taste like vanilla and had an artificial aftertaste.” He notes that it doesn’t mix very well, but says it made him feel great. “Other similar products, like Transparent Labs Mass Gainer, give me an upset stomach. But I felt great after taking Huel Black Edition,” he says.

Promix is our favorite clean protein powder because it’s third-party tested and results are easily viewable on Promix’s website. Those results show this product is tested for heavy metals and verified gluten-free. And beyond these positive results, this protein powder has one of the most simple formulas on our list. Vanilla, for example, has just four ingredients, and Promix doesn’t use any artificial ingredients.

This protein powder, like others on our list, has a solid protein-to-carb ratio for weight loss (25 grams to 7 grams, respectively). A 2020 study found consuming a higher portion of protein versus carbs helped participants lose weight and prevented them from gaining the weight back.

I tried the Vanilla flavor of this protein powder. I enjoyed it for the most part, but it wasn’t quite sweet enough for my taste. And I wish it mixed a little better—there were some clumps after mixing.

One thing to note about Promix is that while it has been third-party tested, it hasn’t been third-party tested for sport specifically. This means it hasn’t been tested for substances banned in athletic competitions. So if you’re an athlete planning to compete, opt for a powder that’s Informed Sport Certified or NSF Certified for Sport.

One of my favorite casein protein powders is Casein+ from Legion Athletics. I chose Casein+ because it’s all-natural, meaning it’s free from artificial sweeteners, flavors, and colors, and it’s third-party tested by Labdoor for purity and potency. This product provides 25 grams of protein per serving and only contains 110 calories, regardless of the flavor you choose. This protein-to-calorie ratio is ideal for weight loss.

Along with whey, casein is a type of protein found in milk and is characterized by its slow digestion and absorption. This prolonged digestion makes it an ideal option for people looking to manage hunger levels and maintain a consistent supply of amino acids over an extended timeframe—such as during sleep or when going a long time between meals. By providing a steady stream of protein to the muscles, casein helps mitigate the risk of muscle breakdown that often accompanies calorie restriction. As a result, incorporating a casein protein powder into your diet can be a strategic move to help support your weight loss goals.

Tester Brandon Lunsford, C.P.T., tried the Dutch Chocolate flavor, saying it reminded him of a dark chocolate bar that isn’t too rich or too sweet. The only downside is that casein protein has a different consistency than whey. It’s generally thicker and often takes longer to dissolve. Lunsford noticed this during his testing, saying the product had a “slightly chalky aftertaste.”

Naked Whey’s Unflavored protein stands out for its simplicity and purity; its single-ingredient formula consists of whey protein concentrate sourced for grass-fed cows. This simplicity aligns with the brand’s commitment to transparency, priding itself on avoiding additives, fillers, or artificial ingredients in its products.

With its neutral taste profile, this protein powder is very versatile, letting you integrate the protein powder seamlessly into your favorite recipes or smoothies without altering the flavor profile. Kessler tried the Unflavored version and says it “has a very slight vanilla taste to it.” He also detected a note of earthiness, but says “It would be really good mixed into a smoothie.” However, he mentions the two-scoop serving size can feel like a lot, so he recommends using extra liquid when blending it.

If you’re someone who prefers a flavored protein powder, you’ll be happy to know Naked also offers five flavored options, including Chocolate, Vanilla, Strawberry, Chocolate Peanut Butter, and Double Chocolate. Naked only uses coconut sugar to sweeten its protein supplements, which isn’t nearly as sweet as artificial sweeteners like sucralose or acesulfame potassium.

We chose Sports Research as our best protein powder for weight loss and muscle gain because it has a solid protein-to-calorie ratio (25 grams to 140 calories), is Informed Sport Certified, is fairly priced at $1.20 per serving, and tastes great, according to testers.

From a nutritional standpoint, Sports Research stacks up well against many of its competitors. The per-serving content for protein (25 grams), calories (140), and carbs (2 grams) compares favorably with most of the choices on our list, although the fat per serving (3.5 grams for Vanilla and 4 grams for Dutch Chocolate) is on the high side. Other ingredients include vitamin D, which has been linked to muscle health in recent research.

Tester Cory Kessler, C.N.C., C.P.T., tried the Creamy Vanilla flavor. “When I mixed it with milk it almost tasted like vanilla ice cream,” he says. “But when I mixed it with water it diluted the flavor, and all I could taste was the sweetness,” he warns. He also notes that it mixed very well, and “wasn’t gritty or clumpy at all.”

Whether from powder or whole food sources, protein aids weight loss mainly by:

Protein powder can be an effective tool in helping you achieve your weight loss goals. Drinking a protein powder shake or smoothie provides a quick, easy way to consume high amounts of protein with a limited amount of calories, fat, and carbohydrates. One of the main benefits of protein powder is that it’s often extremely lean, with a very high ratio of protein to total number of calories. This makes protein powder an efficient way to hit your daily protein target while adhering to your calorie guidelines.

Choose a protein powder with a significant amount of protein, typically around 25 grams per serving. If you have weight loss goals, a whey, soy, or pea protein isolate is likely your best bet since they are ultra-filtered to remove excess carbohydrates and fats.

When you have weight loss goals, it’s best to choose a protein powder with a moderate calorie count per serving, e.g., 100 to 160 calories. You should also ensure the majority of those calories come from protein, as this will best support your weight loss progress. Remember, protein is four calories per gram, so you can expect a supplement that has 25 grams of protein to have around 110 to 120 calories if it’s extremely lean.

It’s important to check the ingredients list of the supplement to ensure the product is free from added sugars or unnecessary fillers. Although these ingredients may contribute to the flavor, sweetness, and creaminess of the supplement, they often come with added calories. It’s generally best to select protein powders with minimal ingredients.

Occasionally, protein powders contain ingredients such as creatine, probiotics, or branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). While these aren’t necessary, it’s important to assess whether these added ingredients align with your health and fitness goals, and whether it’s worth choosing a protein powder that offers these options.

Regardless of your goals, choose a protein powder with a flavor and consistency you enjoy. I know this seems obvious, but if you dislike the taste, then you’re far less likely to use the protein powder on a consistent basis, if at all.

As a certified nutrition coach, I advise my clients to choose a protein powder that’s been third-party tested for quality, purity, and safety, especially when I’m working with athletes. This ensures your supplement is free from contaminants, including banned substances, and is deemed safe for consumption. Third-party testing also holds supplement companies accountable, providing assurance that the ingredients in the product align with the information provided on the supplement facts label.

Whenever you’re purchasing a dietary supplement, you should look for one that aligns with your specific health and fitness goals. With weight loss in mind, it’s typically recommended to avoid products with added sugars, or excessive amounts of carbohydrates and fats. Some consumers may also choose to avoid products with artificial additives, such as sweeteners, flavors, and colors, which are routinely found in protein powder supplements. If you’re looking for an all-natural protein powder with minimal ingredients, consider Transparent Labs 100% Grass-Fed Whey or protein powders from Naked Nutrition.

As a certified nutrition coach, I think it’s important to emphasize that a protein powder isn’t a necessity for weight loss success. However, due to its convenience and effectiveness, it does offer some notable benefits when used as part of a holistic approach to weight loss that includes resistance training, quality sleep, and healthy lifestyle habits. Consuming a high-protein diet, especially during a weight-loss phase, helps manage hunger levels and improves muscle preservation. If a protein powder can help you hit your daily protein targets while still maintaining a calorie deficit, then I think it’s worth incorporating into your regular routine.

Protein shakes are an excellent way to help preserve lean muscle mass when pursuing your weight loss goals. If weight loss is your primary objective, I’d suggest opting for a whey protein isolate, such as Transparent Labs 100% Grass-Fed Whey. This protein powder is incredibly lean, meaning the majority of calories come from protein alone. This can help you achieve your daily protein targets without over-consuming calories from the additional carbohydrates and fats commonly found in a whey protein concentrate.

Weight loss strategies vary from person to person, however, individuals with weight loss goals should aim for at least 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight. (This equates to approximately 0.5 to 0.7 grams of protein per pound of body weight.) This range should provide enough protein to support muscle mass while maintaining a calorie deficit, which is necessary for weight loss.

With protein powder for weight loss, certain protein sources are considered “leaner” than others. For example, whey protein isolates benefit from various kinds of processing and filtration that lower the fat and carbohydrates in the finished product. The main drawback with some plant-based proteins is that they can be naturally higher in carbs. Fortunately, high-quality plant protein powders could deliver comparable results to whey protein in terms of promoting lean body mass.Lean animal proteins include chicken breast, fish, and eggs. Even certain cuts of beef (sirloin) and pork (loin) are considered lean. Greek yogurt, tofu, beans, and lentils are among the non-animal sources of lean protein.

When focusing on weight loss, it’s best to steer clear of calorie-rich beverages such as sugary sodas and sports drinks, fruit juices, and alcohol. Instead, choose options like water, seltzer, black coffee, and unsweetened tea, all of which are essentially calorie-free. Avoiding calorie-dense beverages allows you to allocate those calories to food instead, which should help improve your satiety or feelings of fullness after meals.

There’s no protein that targets belly fat loss specifically. However, prioritizing lean protein, such as a whey protein isolate, can be beneficial for your overall weight loss goals. Whey protein isolates are processed to minimize the carbohydrate and fat content, maximizing the protein-to-calorie ratio of the supplement. This makes them an efficient option to support your intake of dietary protein while maintaining a calorie deficit.

The gold standard business class redemption using British Airways Avios

Picture this: you're seated in a private suite at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, your door clicked shut behind you, a glass of Dom Pérignon on the side table, and a fully flat bed dressed in Westin Heavenly bedding waiting for you. Your partner is in the suite next to yours — and when you lower the center dividing panel, you're sharing a meal in what Qatar Airways calls the "Double Bed" configuration. This is QSuites, and it is, without exaggeration, the single most celebrated business class product in the world. Now here's the number that stops the ChooseFI community cold: a cash ticket in QSuites from New York JFK to Doha DOH typically runs **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's a mortgage payment. That's a family vacation budget. That's real money that compounds in an index fund. With Qatar Avios through the Privilege Club program, that same seat costs **75,000 Avios**. When you do the math against even the conservative cash price of $5,000, you're extracting **6.7 cents per point**. Against the top-end cash price of $10,000, that's **13.3 cents per point** — in a world where most loyalty currencies are "worth" 1 cent each. This is a 6x to 13x multiplier on every point you've earned. Here's what makes this a genuine pricing inefficiency rather than just marketing: Qatar's award chart is fixed and partner-friendly, meaning the number of points required doesn't scale dynamically with cash prices the way most airline programs now do. When demand spikes and cash fares hit $10,000, your award price stays exactly 75,000 Avios. The loyalty program hasn't caught up to the revenue management engine, and that gap is your opportunity. For anyone on the path to financial independence, this is the travel rewards philosophy in its purest form: redirect real spending you're already doing onto the right cards, accumulate points as a byproduct, and convert those points into experiences that would otherwise require liquidating investments. The QSuites redemption is the pinnacle of that system — a **nearly free** business class experience that delivers more luxury per point than almost anything else in the world of travel rewards.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegant once you see it, and once you see it, you'll start recognizing similar patterns everywhere in the loyalty space.

Qatar prices its own flights in its own currency — and that currency is cheap to acquire.

Qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios are the program's native points currency. When Qatar sets award prices for its own operated flights, including QSuites, it prices them in a way that's competitive and fixed — not subject to the dynamic pricing algorithms that have made programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles increasingly unpredictable. Seventy-five thousand Avios for a transatlantic or transoceanic business class seat is a published, stable price. Qatar isn't trying to extract maximum value from every award booking; they want to keep the program attractive to drive loyalty.

The critical insight is this: you don't need to earn Qatar Avios through Qatar flights. You can transfer them directly from credit card programs you're probably already using.

Citi ThankYou Points → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — This is the fastest and cleanest route. Transfers from Citi to Qatar are instant, meaning you can search for availability, confirm the seat is bookable, and transfer in the same session without risk. For anyone holding a Citi Premier or Citi Prestige card, this is a direct pipeline to QSuites.

Capital One Miles → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — A strong secondary option. Capital One's transfer to Qatar takes 2–5 days, so you'll want to confirm availability first and ideally put the seat on a 24-hour hold if possible before initiating the transfer. Venture X and Venture card holders have access to this path.

Marriott Bonvoy Points → Qatar Avios at 3:1 — This is the least efficient path. The 3:1 ratio means you're effectively diluting your Bonvoy points, and transfers take 1–5 days. Use this only as a top-off strategy if you're a few thousand Avios short and have Bonvoy points sitting idle.

This is a huge deal that deserves its own callout. Qatar charges zero fuel surcharges on Qatar-operated award flights. This is not universal — British Airways Avios, for example, can pile on $700+ in carrier-imposed surcharges on longhaul awards. With Qatar Privilege Club, what you see is what you pay: 75,000 Avios plus the government taxes, which are typically modest.

Qatar allows stopovers in Doha and open-jaw routing on award tickets. This means you can build a trip that stops in Doha — giving you access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge, one of the world's premier airport lounges — before continuing to a final destination. The stopover rule turns a single award redemption into a multi-destination experience, a classic FI travel rewards optimization move.

This is the cardinal rule of all transfer-based award bookings: never transfer points until you've confirmed the seat exists. Go to qatarairways.com and run a search using the "Privilege Club" award booking tool. Select Business Class, enter your route (e.g., JFK to DOH), and look for QSuites availability specifically — you'll see the aircraft type and cabin configuration in the search results. QSuites is typically available on Boeing 777-300ER and A380 flights, not all Qatar aircraft, so confirm the product before you get excited.

Qatar Privilege Club opens its award booking window at 361 days in advance. QSuites availability is genuinely limited — this is a Difficulty 2/5 on the availability scale — and the best seats disappear quickly, especially for peak travel periods and popular routes like JFK–DOH. Set a calendar reminder now for exactly 361 days before your target departure date and be ready to book the moment the window opens. This single habit separates people who get QSuites awards from people who watch them disappear.

You'll need 75,000 Qatar Avios per person. Check your current balances across:

Decide your primary transfer source before you need the points. If you're using Capital One, initiate the transfer 5–7 days before you want to book to give yourself buffer time.

If you don't have a Privilege Club account, create one at qatarairways.com/privilege-club — it's free and takes minutes. Once you have your account number, you can link it as a transfer destination in your Citi, Capital One, or Marriott account.

Once you've confirmed availability and are ready to book, log into your credit card rewards portal and initiate the transfer to your Qatar Privilege Club account number. For Citi, this will post instantly. For Capital One, monitor your Avios balance over the next 2–5 days.

Return to qatarairways.com, log into your Privilege Club account, and book the award using your Avios balance. Have your passport and payment method ready for the taxes and fees. Confirm the aircraft type one final time at booking to ensure you're on a QSuites-equipped aircraft.

If you can't find two seats together, try splitting the booking into two single-seat reservations, then request to link them. Also try ±3 days on either side of your target dates — availability patterns are uneven. Calling Qatar's Privilege Club phone line (rather than booking online) occasionally surfaces inventory not shown on the website.

British Airways Avios uses a distance-based award chart rather than a flat-rate chart, which creates a pricing inefficiency on long-haul routes operated by Qatar Airways. While BA prices short-haul flights competitively, flights over 4,000 miles to Qatar and beyond land in a pricing band that dramatically undervalues the QSuites product. Qatar Airways is a oneworld alliance member, which means BA Avios can book any Qatar-operated award flight. The key insight is that you are booking through BA's system using BA's pricing, but flying on Qatar's hardware — and Qatar's business class product is in a completely different league than BA's Club World. This mismatch between the booking partner's award chart and the operating airline's product quality is exactly what makes this a sweet spot.

Let's build a real booking so the numbers stop being abstract.

The Route: New York JFK → Doha DOH on Qatar Airways, Boeing 777-300ER, QSuites Business Class.

Cash Price: A one-way QSuites ticket on this route runs roughly $5,000–$8,000 depending on timing and booking window. For a couple, you're looking at $10,000–$16,000 in cash — a number that probably makes the FI-minded reader physically uncomfortable.

Award Price: 75,000 Qatar Avios per person, one-way. Taxes and fees on Qatar-operated awards are minimal — typically under $100 — because Qatar charges no fuel surcharges. A couple flies QSuites for 150,000 Avios plus roughly $150 in taxes total.

The CPP: At the midpoint cash value of $6,500, you're getting 8.7 cents per Avios — nearly nine times what most people assume a loyalty point is worth. At $10,000, you're at 13.3 cents per point. Even at the conservative end, 6.7 cents per point makes this one of the top redemptions in the entire travel rewards ecosystem.

You arrive at JFK and access Qatar's partner lounge before departure — a preview of what's to come. Once aboard, you're shown to a fully enclosed private suite with a sliding door, direct aisle access from every seat, a large personal screen, and a seat that converts to a lie-flat bed stretching over 6 feet. The bedding is genuine Westin Heavenly quality. You and your travel companion request the Double Bed configuration — the center divider lowers, and you're sharing a full-width sleeping surface mid-flight.

Dining is a la carte, on-demand — no set meal times. The wine list is legitimate. The service is attentive without being intrusive.

If you've added a Doha stopover to your ticket, you deplane into Al Mourjan Business Lounge — a cavernous, beautifully designed space with dedicated dining, shower suites, and quiet zones. It is, consistently, one of the top-rated airport lounges on earth.

This is the experience your 75,000 points buy. No amount of economy class upgrades gets you here.
